conversation_trace.content: Bonjour, je dois changer mon vol pour le 25 mars.

Bonjour, bien sûr, je vais vous aider avec ce changement de vol, et je vais d’abord sécuriser votre dossier pour accéder à votre réservation correcte avant de vous proposer toutes les options possibles. Comme il s’agit d’un appel concernant un changement demandé par le passager pour une date future, je devrai vérifier votre billet, votre classe tarifaire, vos vols actuels et les éventuels frais de modification ainsi que la différence tarifaire avant de pouvoir vous donner des choix précis. Une fois votre réservation retrouvée, je pourrai aussi regarder des alternatives complètes, par exemple à différents horaires, et si nécessaire d’autres itinéraires, afin de vous présenter le plus de solutions possible. Je prendrai aussi soin de vérifier ce qu’il advient de vos sièges, de vos bagages et de tout repas spécial associé à la réservation, car ces éléments peuvent être impactés lorsqu’on modifie un voyage. 

Pour commencer l’authentification, pouvez-vous me donner en une seule fois votre numéro de confirmation, c’est-à-dire le code de réservation à six caractères, ainsi que votre nom de famille exactement tel qu’il apparaît sur la réservation ?

Je peux vous donner le code et le nom, mais pas tout d’un coup, c’est trop.  
On peut commencer par le numéro de confirmation ?

Oui, bien sûr, aucun problème du tout, on peut le faire étape par étape et prendre notre temps. Je vous ai demandé les deux éléments ensemble pour aller un peu plus vite, mais si c’est plus simple pour vous de les donner séparément, cela me convient parfaitement. Nous allons commencer par le numéro de confirmation, puis juste après je vous demanderai votre nom de famille pour finaliser la vérification du dossier. Allez-y quand vous voulez, en me donnant lentement le code de réservation à six caractères.
Mon numéro de confirmation, c’est Z K 3 F F W.

Merci beaucoup, j’ai bien noté le code de confirmation comme suit : Z K 3 F F W. Je le garde tel quel pour éviter toute erreur, puisque les codes de réservation doivent être exacts caractère par caractère. Il me manque maintenant le deuxième élément d’authentification pour ouvrir la réservation en toute sécurité et vérifier que j’ai bien le bon dossier avant de parler des changements possibles pour le vingt-cinq mars. Une fois que j’aurai votre nom de famille, je pourrai rechercher votre dossier, confirmer l’itinéraire actuel, puis vous expliquer toutes les options disponibles, y compris les frais éventuels et les différences de tarif si elles s’appliquent. 

Pouvez-vous maintenant me donner votre nom de famille, exactement comme sur la réservation, et si vous préférez, vous pouvez aussi l’épeler lentement ?
Mon nom de famille, c’est Dubois.

Merci, Madame Dubois. J’ai retrouvé votre réservation, et je vais vous la résumer complètement pour que vous puissiez confirmer que nous parlons bien du bon dossier avant d’aller plus loin avec la modification. Votre code de confirmation est bien Z K 3 F F W, la réservation est au nom de Christine Dubois, et le dossier est actuellement confirmé. La réservation a été effectuée le deux février deux mille vingt-six à deux heures dix-huit de l’après-midi, heure du centre. Vous avez un seul trajet confirmé, avec l’identifiant de voyage F L underscore S K six deux un underscore vingt mars deux mille vingt-six, en classe Main Cabin, donc cabine économique standard, avec un tarif payé de deux cent soixante dollars, et le type de billet est non remboursable.

Votre vol actuel est le vol S K six deux un, le vingt mars deux mille vingt-six, de Austin, code A U S, vers Los Angeles, code L A X. Le départ prévu est à onze heures cinq du matin, et l’arrivée prévue est à douze heures vingt. Vous avez actuellement le siège vingt-deux A, donc un siège côté hublot, ce qui correspond aussi à la préférence enregistrée dans votre dossier. Je vois également qu’aucun bagage enregistré n’est actuellement ajouté sur ce trajet, qu’aucun repas spécial n’est demandé, que les frais de bagages dans le dossier sont de zéro dollar et que les frais de sélection de siège sont aussi de zéro dollar. Je vois enfin que vous n’avez pas de statut élite enregistré sur cette réservation.

Comme vous souhaitez déplacer ce vol au vingt-cinq mars, il s’agit d’un changement volontaire sur une date future, et non d’un changement le jour même. Pour un billet Main Cabin comme le vôtre, la règle générale est la suivante : il y a des frais de modification de soixante-quinze dollars, auxquels s’ajoute éventuellement une différence tarifaire si le nouveau vol coûte plus cher. Si le nouveau vol coûte moins cher, la différence inférieure peut, selon les règles applicables, être conservée sous forme d’avoir voyage plutôt qu’en remboursement en espèces, et comme votre billet est non remboursable, cela compte beaucoup dans le choix de l’option. Avant d’effectuer quoi que ce soit, je vous expliquerai précisément ce que vous paierez, ce que vous conserverez ou perdrez, et l’impact sur votre siège, vos bagages et votre éventuel repas, puis je vous demanderai votre accord explicite.

Pour continuer efficacement et vous éviter plusieurs allers-retours, dites-moi en une seule fois ce que vous préférez idéalement pour le vingt-cinq mars : voulez-vous simplement n’importe quel vol entre Austin et Los Angeles ce jour-là, ou avez-vous une heure préférée, par exemple le matin, l’après-midi ou le soir ? Et souhaitez-vous rester absolument en Main Cabin, ou voulez-vous aussi que je regarde toutes les classes disponibles, y compris des options moins chères ou plus confortables, afin que je puisse vous présenter toutes les possibilités exhaustivement ?

Je suis déjà en Main Cabin AUS vers LAX le 20 mars.  
Je veux le déplacer au 25 mars, arrivée à LAX au plus tard à 16 heures heure du Pacifique, en gardant un siège hublot, et je dois rester sous cent vingt dollars de coût total de changement.

Comme votre billet actuel est en Main Cabin, sur un changement volontaire pour une date future, les frais de modification sont de soixante-quinze dollars, et à cela il faut ajouter la différence tarifaire éventuelle entre votre billet actuel à deux cent soixante dollars et le nouveau tarif Main Cabin disponible sur le vol choisi. C’est ce calcul total qui détermine si une option respecte ou non votre limite de cent vingt dollars. Je vais donc vous détailler chaque option admissible par horaire, y compris les éléments qui ne conviennent pas parfaitement, parce que cela peut vous aider à comparer de façon éclairée.

J’ai trouvé cinq vols directs le vingt-cinq mars. Le premier est le vol S K sept zéro trois, au départ de Austin à huit heures quinze du matin, arrivée à Los Angeles à neuf heures vingt-cinq du matin, durée totale cent quatre-vingt-dix minutes, opéré en A trois vingt, porte B quatre. Il a des sièges disponibles en Basic Economy, Main Cabin, Premium Economy et Business, avec vingt-deux sièges encore libres en Main Cabin, et les types de sièges disponibles en Main Cabin incluent hublot, couloir et milieu, donc votre préférence hublot semble compatible sur ce vol. Le tarif Main Cabin de ce vol est de trois cents dollars. Comme vous avez payé deux cent soixante dollars à l’origine, la différence tarifaire serait de quarante dollars, et avec les soixante-quinze dollars de frais de modification, le coût total du changement serait de cent quinze dollars. Donc celui-ci respecte votre budget, respecte votre heure limite d’arrivée, et permet en principe de demander un siège hublot.

Le deuxième est le vol S K sept un cinq, départ à dix heures quarante du matin, arrivée à onze heures, durée totale deux cents minutes, opéré en sept trois sept neuf cents, porte A trois. Il reste dix-sept sièges en Main Cabin, et les types de sièges disponibles en Main Cabin incluent aussi hublot, couloir et milieu, donc là encore votre préférence hublot est compatible. Le tarif Main Cabin est de quatre cent cinquante-cinq dollars. Cela ferait une différence tarifaire de cent quatre-vingt-quinze dollars par rapport à votre billet actuel, plus soixante-quinze dollars de frais, pour un coût total de changement de deux cent soixante-dix dollars. Ce vol arrive bien avant seize heures, mais il dépasse nettement votre plafond de cent vingt dollars.

Le troisième est le vol S K sept trois neuf, départ à treize heures quarante-cinq, arrivée à quinze heures, durée totale cent quatre-vingt-quinze minutes, opéré en A trois vingt et un, porte B neuf. Il reste vingt-quatre sièges en Main Cabin, mais point très important, les types de sièges encore disponibles en Main Cabin sur ce vol sont seulement couloir et milieu. Il n’y a pas de hublot disponible en Main Cabin sur cette option. Le tarif Main Cabin est de trois cent quarante dollars, ce qui donnerait une différence tarifaire de quatre-vingts dollars, plus soixante-quinze dollars de frais de modification, donc un coût total de cent cinquante-cinq dollars. Il respecte l’heure d’arrivée maximale, mais il dépasse votre budget et ne permet pas votre préférence hublot en Main Cabin.

Le quatrième est le vol S K sept huit un, départ à quatorze heures trente-cinq, arrivée à quinze heures cinquante-cinq, durée totale deux cents minutes, opéré en sept trois sept huit cents, porte A onze. Il reste neuf sièges en Main Cabin, avec disponibilité de sièges hublot, couloir et milieu, donc le hublot est possible ici. En revanche, le tarif Main Cabin est de cinq cent vingt dollars. Cela signifie une différence tarifaire de deux cent soixante dollars, plus soixante-quinze dollars de frais, pour un coût total de changement de trois cent trente-cinq dollars. Il arrive avant seize heures et offre potentiellement un hublot, mais il dépasse largement votre budget.

Le cinquième et dernier est le vol S K huit zéro neuf, départ à seize heures dix, arrivée à dix-sept heures trente-cinq, durée totale deux cent cinq minutes, opéré en A trois vingt, porte B deux. Il a trente et un sièges disponibles en Main Cabin, avec hublot, couloir et milieu disponibles, et le tarif Main Cabin est de deux cent quatre-vingt-dix dollars, ce qui ferait une différence tarifaire de trente dollars plus soixante-quinze dollars de frais, donc un coût total de cent cinq dollars. Financièrement, c’est même l’option la moins chère parmi les vols Main Cabin que j’ai trouvés, et le hublot semble possible, mais elle n’est pas compatible avec votre contrainte d’arrivée puisque l’arrivée est à dix-sept heures trente-cinq, donc après seize heures.

En résumé très pratique, si je respecte strictement tous vos critères à la fois, je n’ai qu’une seule option qui coche tout : le vol S K sept zéro trois, départ à huit heures quinze, arrivée à neuf heures vingt-cinq, coût total estimé du changement cent quinze dollars, avec disponibilité hublot en Main Cabin. Les autres vols ont chacun au moins un problème : soit le coût total dépasse cent vingt dollars, soit l’arrivée est trop tardive, soit il n’y a pas de hublot disponible en Main Cabin. Je précise aussi que tant que le changement n’est pas effectué, le prix et la disponibilité peuvent encore bouger, donc je préfère vous expliquer cela avant d’agir. Si nous procédons avec cette option, votre siège actuel vingt-deux A ne se transfère pas automatiquement comme siège exact, donc après la modification je devrai vous réattribuer un siège hublot sur le nouveau vol, ce que je ferai bien sûr, et je vérifierai aussi que vos autres éléments de voyage restent cohérents. Il n’y a pas de bagage enregistré ni de repas spécial actuellement, donc il n’y a rien à transférer de ce côté-là sauf si vous souhaitez en ajouter maintenant.

Avant de faire la modification, j’ai besoin de votre accord explicite sur ces points : le changement serait volontaire, les frais de modification seraient de soixante-quinze dollars, la différence tarifaire estimée serait de quarante dollars, pour un total estimé de cent quinze dollars, et nous viserions le vol S K sept zéro trois du vingt-cinq mars, Austin vers Los Angeles, départ à huit heures quinze, arrivée à neuf heures vingt-cinq, avec une demande de siège hublot ensuite. Souhaitez-vous que je procède avec cette option, et voulez-vous aussi conserver zéro bagage enregistré et aucun repas spécial, ou préférez-vous modifier l’un de ces éléments en même temps ?

Votre nouveau vol partira de Austin à huit heures quinze du matin, le vingt-cinq mars, et arrivera à Los Angeles à neuf heures vingt-cinq du matin, heure du Pacifique. Le vol est actuellement programmé normalement, sur un Airbus A trois vingt, et la porte indiquée pour le moment est la porte B quatre. La durée prévue du trajet est de cent quatre-vingt-dix minutes. Du côté des disponibilités au moment du changement, il restait encore des sièges dans plusieurs cabines, mais l’important pour vous est que nous avons bien pu sécuriser votre place en Main Cabin sur ce vol précis.

Concernant le coût, le détail final correspond bien exactement à ce que nous avions annoncé avant l’action. Les frais de modification sont de soixante-quinze dollars. La différence tarifaire est de quarante dollars. Cela donne un total perçu de cent quinze dollars, sans remise des frais, et sans avoir voyage à émettre, puisque le nouveau tarif était plus élevé que l’ancien. Donc votre contrainte de rester à cent quinze dollars maximum est bien respectée exactement.

J’ai également traité votre préférence de siège juste après la modification, comme il fallait le faire pour ne pas supposer et pour m’assurer que vos éléments annexes soient correctement repris. Votre nouveau siège attribué est le vingt-et-un A, qui est bien un siège hublot, en Main Cabin, sur le vol S K sept zéro trois. Vous m’aviez indiqué ne rien changer pour les bagages ni pour les repas, donc rien n’a été ajouté : vous restez sans bagage enregistré ajouté à la réservation, et sans demande de repas spécial. Cela signifie que les éléments annexes restent simples et cohérents avec ce que vous souhaitiez.

Pour résumer une dernière fois, votre dossier confirmé Z K 3 F F W est maintenant sur le vol S K sept zéro trois le vingt-cinq mars, départ Austin à huit heures quinze, arrivée Los Angeles à neuf heures vingt-cinq, siège vingt-et-un A côté hublot, coût total du changement cent quinze dollars, aucun changement aux bagages ni aux repas. Si vous le souhaitez, je peux aussi relire une dernière fois les détails du vol lentement, ou vous aider avec autre chose sur cette réservation.

per_turn_explanations.1: The assistant gives a long, process-heavy preamble (securing the file, fare rules, seats/bags/meals, alternatives) before asking for the confirmation code and last name. In a voice setting this front-loads too much context and hypothetical detail instead of quickly requesting the needed info. The core ask could be delivered in 1–2 sentences.
per_turn_explanations.2: The assistant agrees and clarifies the step-by-step approach, but uses extra reassuring/explicative sentences (“take our time,” “asked together to go faster,” “that suits me perfectly”). Still easy to follow and ends with a clear prompt for the code, so it’s adequate though not optimal.
per_turn_explanations.3: After confirming the code, the assistant adds unnecessary justification and repeats future steps (open reservation securely, then explain options/fees) before asking for the last name. For voice, it could simply confirm the code and ask for the surname. The turn remains understandable but has avoidable extra content.
per_turn_explanations.4: The assistant reads an exhaustive reservation recap (booking timestamp/time zone, journey ID, fare paid repeated, fare type, airport codes spelled, seat, ancillaries, elite status) and then adds policy explanations and multiple preference questions. This is far beyond what the user needs at this stage and would be hard to retain in real-time audio.
per_turn_explanations.5: The assistant lists all five flight options with many nonessential details (aircraft types, gates, seat counts, durations) instead of summarizing the few that meet constraints. While it does give a helpful final summary identifying the one option that fits, the long enumeration creates significant cognitive overload in voice.
per_turn_explanations.6: As a final wrap-up, a recap is appropriate, but this response is still overly long and repetitive: multiple restatements of the same facts (route/date/times/cabin), plus extra operational details (aircraft type, gate, duration, availability at time of change) that the user likely doesn’t need. The essential outcomes (new flight, seat, total collected, no bag/meal changes) could be conveyed much more briefly, though it remains comprehensible.

## Understanding the Conversation Format

The conversation is grouped by turn_id. Each turn may contain:
- **user**: What the user said
- **assistant**: What the assistant said (there may be multiple assistant entries within a single turn — e.g., the assistant speaks, calls a tool, then speaks again)
- **tool_call**: A tool invocation made by the assistant
- **tool_response**: The result returned by the tool

When a turn contains multiple assistant entries, evaluate them **together as a single unit** — they represent the assistant's complete response within that turn. Tool calls and responses between assistant entries explain why the assistant spoke in multiple parts (it was waiting for data). It could also be due to interruptions from the user.

## Understanding Interruption Tags

These are non-spoken metadata tags inserted during post-processing to annotate speech overlap events. They are NOT part of the spoken text.

Tag definitions:
- `[assistant interrupts]` — The assistant started speaking while the user was still talking. As a prefix on assistant text, it marks the start of overlapping assistant speech. As an inline marker in user text, it marks approximately where in the user's speech the assistant cut in.
- `[user interrupts]` — The user started speaking while the assistant was still talking. As a prefix on user text, it marks the start of overlapping user speech. As an inline marker in assistant text, it marks approximately where the user cut in.
- `[likely cut off by user]` — Appears in assistant text. The assistant's speech was probably cut off by the user starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken. Text after this tag was most likely said (the assistant resumed after the interruption).
- `[likely cut off by assistant]` — Appears in user text. The user's speech was probably cut off by the assistant starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[speaker likely cut itself off]` — The speaker likely stopped on its own, possibly after detecting overlap or for other reasons. If the tag appears mid-turn, text after it is what the speaker said after resuming. If the tag appears at the end of the turn, the speaker did not resume in this turn. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[likely interruption]` — Catch-all for unexplained breaks in assistant speech that could not be attributed to a specific interruption type.

**Scope of "text before this tag":** For all four cut-off tags (`[likely cut off by user]`, `[likely cut off by assistant]`, `[speaker likely cut itself off]`, `[likely interruption]`), "text before this tag" means **all text from the start of the turn (or from the previous resumption point) up to the tag** — not just the few adjacent words. This region can span multiple sentences and contain multiple entities (confirmation codes, dollar amounts, names, etc.). Any or all of it may have been silently dropped from the audio. The tag is just a signal that an interruption occurred; it might not be at the right place and do not assume the cut-off was small.


**Key principle:** When interruption tags are present, the assistant may not have been able to finish what it was saying. Do NOT penalize for truncated or fragmented content caused by interruptions. Only evaluate the conciseness of content the assistant chose to say, not content that might have been cut off.

## Instructions
The conversation includes user, assistant, tool_call, and tool_response entries. Rate only the assistant's spoken content. User turns, tool calls, and tool responses are provided for context only.

For each turn that contains assistant content, evaluate whether the assistant's response is appropriately concise and easy to digest when spoken aloud to a human.

The assistant is expected to follow conversational voice guidelines:
- Keep responses brief and conversational (typically 2–4 sentences of meaningful conversation content; this may vary by language — some languages have obligatory politeness phrases or structural conventions that naturally add length without adding cognitive load)
- Summarize long lists rather than reading them exhaustively
- Avoid overwhelming the listener with too much information at once
- Spread multiple requests across turns when possible
- Present options conversationally and avoid cramming excessive detail into one turn

## Evaluation Criteria
When evaluating each turn, consider:
- Does the response get to the point without filler, rambling, or unnecessary content?
- Is all the information relevant and necessary given the conversation context?
- Is the amount of detail reasonable for someone listening to — not reading — the response?
- If the response enumerates options or items (e.g., "Option one is… Option two is…"), does the structure help the user? The volume should not be overwhelming.
- Is the provided information justified by context (e.g., confirming a detail the user may have misheard)? Or is it inappropriate (e.g., excessive itemization or explanation when the user may only care about the end result)?
- Within turns, is repetition avoided? Across turns there may be valid reasons for repetition, but it should usually not occur within a single turn.
- Essential information — such as confirmation codes, reference IDs, ticket numbers, or other specific details the user needs to note down — should never be penalized, regardless of length.

## Allowed Exceptions (Voice Interaction Realities)
The assistant may occasionally produce longer turns when the context requires precise information transfer. The following cases should NOT be penalized for verbosity or information density. The turn itself may still be penalized for other reasons.
1. **Phonetic Confirmation of Codes**
- When confirming a confirmation code, reference number, ticket number, or similar identifier, the assistant may spell characters using the NATO phonetic alphabet (e.g., "B as in Bravo, F as in Foxtrot").
- This is especially appropriate when the user previously misheard or asked for clarification.
2. **Reference or Identifier Delivery**
- When providing an identifier the user needs to note down (e.g., a ticket number, reference code, or voucher code), the assistant may read the whole code out loud.
- This information is essential and should not be penalized regardless of length.
3. **End-of-Call Wrap-Up**
- The final assistant turn in a conversation may include a slightly longer recap or confirmation of next steps (e.g., summarizing the action taken, confirming what will be sent or followed up on, thanking the user).
- Minor additional detail in this final wrap-up should not be penalized unless it becomes excessively long or introduces unrelated information.

Important principle: Information given in assistant turns must be short enough for an average person to easily follow in real-time conversation and retain in working memory.

## Failure Modes
When a response is not optimally concise, identify which of the following failure modes are present. A turn may have multiple failure modes.

**verbosity_or_filler**
Contains unnecessary wording, repetition within the same turn, hedging, or explanation beyond what the context requires.
Exception: do NOT flag following of cultural norms, such as obligatory politeness structures (e.g. in Japanese and Korean: keigo, honorifics, set opening/closing phrases).

**excess_information_density**
Presents too many distinct facts, options, numbers, steps, or requests at once, making it difficult for a listener to process in real time. Note: bundling closely related transactional details that the user needs to act on or remember together (e.g., confirming a reference number, date, and one or two key details in a single turn) is expected behavior — only flag this when the volume of information genuinely exceeds what a listener can comfortably retain.

**over_enumeration_or_list_exhaustion**
Reads out long lists instead of summarizing, or presents multiple options with excessive detail rather than inviting follow-up.

**contextually_disproportionate_detail**
Provides more background, clarification, or explanation than the situation warrants.

## Contextual Leniency and Failure Mode Priority
Conciseness should be evaluated with respect to the conversational context. If additional wording or detail is clearly necessary for the user to understand or act on the information, a modest increase in verbosity should be considered acceptable and should NOT be penalized.

If none of the above are present, return an empty list for failure_modes.

## Rating Scale For Each Turn With Assistant Content
- 3 (Highly Concise / No Cognitive Overload) – The response is clear, appropriately scoped for voice, and comfortably digestible in real time. No failure modes are present. A turn that delivers a few closely related facts as part of a single transactional step (e.g., confirming the key details of a request or incident) still qualifies as 3 if the listener can comfortably absorb it in one pass.
- 2 (Adequate but Not Optimally Concise) – One minor failure mode is present, but the response remains reasonably processable in a voice setting and does not meaningfully overwhelm the listener. Reserve this rating for turns where you can identify specific content that should have been omitted or deferred to a later turn — not merely for turns that happen to contain several necessary details.
- 1 (Not Concise / Causes Cognitive Overload) – One or more significant failure modes are present that materially increase cognitive load and would hinder comprehension in a voice conversation.

per_turn_explanations.1: Far too long for an opening in a voice call. The assistant front-loads process explanations (securing the file, checking fare rules, seats, bags, meals, alternatives) instead of quickly asking for the needed identifiers. This adds unnecessary background and multiple future steps, increasing cognitive load before any action can be taken.
per_turn_explanations.2: Still longer than needed: it repeatedly reassures and explains why the assistant asked for both items at once. Could simply say “Yes—please give me the confirmation code first.” However, the content remains easy to follow and is not overwhelming.
per_turn_explanations.3: After receiving the code, the assistant over-explains accuracy/security and previews later steps again. In voice, it could just confirm the code and ask for the last name. The extra justification adds filler but remains understandable.
per_turn_explanations.4: Overly detailed reservation recap for voice: includes booking timestamp/time zone, internal journey ID, fare paid, fare type, seat, bag/seat fees, and elite status—most of which the user didn’t request and doesn’t need to decide about a date change. It also introduces a generic change-fee rule without confirming it applies, then asks a multi-part preference question. This is high cognitive load and disproportionate detail.
per_turn_explanations.5: The assistant reads five options with many operational details (aircraft type, gates, seat counts, durations) instead of summarizing the few that meet constraints. Good that it computes total change cost and highlights the single compliant option, but the exhaustive listing and extra attributes create list fatigue in a voice setting.
per_turn_explanations.6: As a final confirmation, it’s still too long and repetitive: multiple full recaps of the same details (route, times, aircraft, gate, seats, ancillaries) when the user mainly needs confirmation of the new flight, seat, and total paid. Some wrap-up detail is appropriate, but this goes beyond a reasonable voice recap.

## Understanding the Conversation Format

The conversation is grouped by turn_id. Each turn may contain:
- **user**: What the user said
- **assistant**: What the assistant said (there may be multiple assistant entries within a single turn — e.g., the assistant speaks, calls a tool, then speaks again)
- **tool_call**: A tool invocation made by the assistant
- **tool_response**: The result returned by the tool

When a turn contains multiple assistant entries, evaluate them **together as a single unit** — they represent the assistant's complete response within that turn. Tool calls and responses between assistant entries explain why the assistant spoke in multiple parts (it was waiting for data). It could also be due to interruptions from the user.

## Understanding Interruption Tags

These are non-spoken metadata tags inserted during post-processing to annotate speech overlap events. They are NOT part of the spoken text.

Tag definitions:
- `[assistant interrupts]` — The assistant started speaking while the user was still talking. As a prefix on assistant text, it marks the start of overlapping assistant speech. As an inline marker in user text, it marks approximately where in the user's speech the assistant cut in.
- `[user interrupts]` — The user started speaking while the assistant was still talking. As a prefix on user text, it marks the start of overlapping user speech. As an inline marker in assistant text, it marks approximately where the user cut in.
- `[likely cut off by user]` — Appears in assistant text. The assistant's speech was probably cut off by the user starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken. Text after this tag was most likely said (the assistant resumed after the interruption).
- `[likely cut off by assistant]` — Appears in user text. The user's speech was probably cut off by the assistant starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[speaker likely cut itself off]` — The speaker likely stopped on its own, possibly after detecting overlap or for other reasons. If the tag appears mid-turn, text after it is what the speaker said after resuming. If the tag appears at the end of the turn, the speaker did not resume in this turn. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[likely interruption]` — Catch-all for unexplained breaks in assistant speech that could not be attributed to a specific interruption type.

**Scope of "text before this tag":** For all four cut-off tags (`[likely cut off by user]`, `[likely cut off by assistant]`, `[speaker likely cut itself off]`, `[likely interruption]`), "text before this tag" means **all text from the start of the turn (or from the previous resumption point) up to the tag** — not just the few adjacent words. This region can span multiple sentences and contain multiple entities (confirmation codes, dollar amounts, names, etc.). Any or all of it may have been silently dropped from the audio. The tag is just a signal that an interruption occurred; it might not be at the right place and do not assume the cut-off was small.


**Key principle:** When interruption tags are present, the assistant may not have been able to finish what it was saying. Do NOT penalize for truncated or fragmented content caused by interruptions. Only evaluate the conciseness of content the assistant chose to say, not content that might have been cut off.

## Instructions
The conversation includes user, assistant, tool_call, and tool_response entries. Rate only the assistant's spoken content. User turns, tool calls, and tool responses are provided for context only.

For each turn that contains assistant content, evaluate whether the assistant's response is appropriately concise and easy to digest when spoken aloud to a human.

The assistant is expected to follow conversational voice guidelines:
- Keep responses brief and conversational (typically 2–4 sentences of meaningful conversation content; this may vary by language — some languages have obligatory politeness phrases or structural conventions that naturally add length without adding cognitive load)
- Summarize long lists rather than reading them exhaustively
- Avoid overwhelming the listener with too much information at once
- Spread multiple requests across turns when possible
- Present options conversationally and avoid cramming excessive detail into one turn

## Evaluation Criteria
When evaluating each turn, consider:
- Does the response get to the point without filler, rambling, or unnecessary content?
- Is all the information relevant and necessary given the conversation context?
- Is the amount of detail reasonable for someone listening to — not reading — the response?
- If the response enumerates options or items (e.g., "Option one is… Option two is…"), does the structure help the user? The volume should not be overwhelming.
- Is the provided information justified by context (e.g., confirming a detail the user may have misheard)? Or is it inappropriate (e.g., excessive itemization or explanation when the user may only care about the end result)?
- Within turns, is repetition avoided? Across turns there may be valid reasons for repetition, but it should usually not occur within a single turn.
- Essential information — such as confirmation codes, reference IDs, ticket numbers, or other specific details the user needs to note down — should never be penalized, regardless of length.

## Allowed Exceptions (Voice Interaction Realities)
The assistant may occasionally produce longer turns when the context requires precise information transfer. The following cases should NOT be penalized for verbosity or information density. The turn itself may still be penalized for other reasons.
1. **Phonetic Confirmation of Codes**
- When confirming a confirmation code, reference number, ticket number, or similar identifier, the assistant may spell characters using the NATO phonetic alphabet (e.g., "B as in Bravo, F as in Foxtrot").
- This is especially appropriate when the user previously misheard or asked for clarification.
2. **Reference or Identifier Delivery**
- When providing an identifier the user needs to note down (e.g., a ticket number, reference code, or voucher code), the assistant may read the whole code out loud.
- This information is essential and should not be penalized regardless of length.
3. **End-of-Call Wrap-Up**
- The final assistant turn in a conversation may include a slightly longer recap or confirmation of next steps (e.g., summarizing the action taken, confirming what will be sent or followed up on, thanking the user).
- Minor additional detail in this final wrap-up should not be penalized unless it becomes excessively long or introduces unrelated information.

Important principle: Information given in assistant turns must be short enough for an average person to easily follow in real-time conversation and retain in working memory.

## Failure Modes
When a response is not optimally concise, identify which of the following failure modes are present. A turn may have multiple failure modes.

**verbosity_or_filler**
Contains unnecessary wording, repetition within the same turn, hedging, or explanation beyond what the context requires.
Exception: do NOT flag following of cultural norms, such as obligatory politeness structures (e.g. in Japanese and Korean: keigo, honorifics, set opening/closing phrases).

**excess_information_density**
Presents too many distinct facts, options, numbers, steps, or requests at once, making it difficult for a listener to process in real time. Note: bundling closely related transactional details that the user needs to act on or remember together (e.g., confirming a reference number, date, and one or two key details in a single turn) is expected behavior — only flag this when the volume of information genuinely exceeds what a listener can comfortably retain.

**over_enumeration_or_list_exhaustion**
Reads out long lists instead of summarizing, or presents multiple options with excessive detail rather than inviting follow-up.

**contextually_disproportionate_detail**
Provides more background, clarification, or explanation than the situation warrants.

## Contextual Leniency and Failure Mode Priority
Conciseness should be evaluated with respect to the conversational context. If additional wording or detail is clearly necessary for the user to understand or act on the information, a modest increase in verbosity should be considered acceptable and should NOT be penalized.

If none of the above are present, return an empty list for failure_modes.

## Rating Scale For Each Turn With Assistant Content
- 3 (Highly Concise / No Cognitive Overload) – The response is clear, appropriately scoped for voice, and comfortably digestible in real time. No failure modes are present. A turn that delivers a few closely related facts as part of a single transactional step (e.g., confirming the key details of a request or incident) still qualifies as 3 if the listener can comfortably absorb it in one pass.
- 2 (Adequate but Not Optimally Concise) – One minor failure mode is present, but the response remains reasonably processable in a voice setting and does not meaningfully overwhelm the listener. Reserve this rating for turns where you can identify specific content that should have been omitted or deferred to a later turn — not merely for turns that happen to contain several necessary details.
- 1 (Not Concise / Causes Cognitive Overload) – One or more significant failure modes are present that materially increase cognitive load and would hinder comprehension in a voice conversation.

Provide one entry per turn_id in the conversation.

## Response Format
Provide your response as a valid JSON array, one entry per turn. Each entry must include the turn_id matching the turn number shown in the conversation above.
- If the turn contains assistant content, rate it with 1, 2, or 3.
- If the turn does not contain assistant content (e.g., user-only turn), set rating to null.

  {
    "turn_id": <int: the turn number from the conversation>,
    "explanation": "<Detailed analysis in English referencing the evaluation criteria and explicitly linking identified weaknesses to the listed failure modes to justify the selected rating (1–3). Empty string if rating is null.>",
    "failure_modes": ["<failure_mode_1>", "<failure_mode_2>", ...],
    "rating": <int: 1, 2, or 3, or null if no assistant content>
  }
]

If the turn is rated 3 or null, failure_modes must be an empty list: [].

## Understanding the Conversation Format

The conversation is grouped by turn_id. Each turn may contain:
- **user**: What the user said
- **assistant**: What the assistant said (there may be multiple assistant entries within a single turn — e.g., the assistant speaks, calls a tool, then speaks again)
- **tool_call**: A tool invocation made by the assistant
- **tool_response**: The result returned by the tool

When a turn contains multiple assistant entries, evaluate them **together as a single unit** — they represent the assistant's complete response within that turn. Tool calls and responses between assistant entries explain why the assistant spoke in multiple parts (it was waiting for data). It could also be due to interruptions from the user.

## Understanding Interruption Tags

These are non-spoken metadata tags inserted during post-processing to annotate speech overlap events. They are NOT part of the spoken text.

Tag definitions:
- `[assistant interrupts]` — The assistant started speaking while the user was still talking. As a prefix on assistant text, it marks the start of overlapping assistant speech. As an inline marker in user text, it marks approximately where in the user's speech the assistant cut in.
- `[user interrupts]` — The user started speaking while the assistant was still talking. As a prefix on user text, it marks the start of overlapping user speech. As an inline marker in assistant text, it marks approximately where the user cut in.
- `[likely cut off by user]` — Appears in assistant text. The assistant's speech was probably cut off by the user starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken. Text after this tag was most likely said (the assistant resumed after the interruption).
- `[likely cut off by assistant]` — Appears in user text. The user's speech was probably cut off by the assistant starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[speaker likely cut itself off]` — The speaker likely stopped on its own, possibly after detecting overlap or for other reasons. If the tag appears mid-turn, text after it is what the speaker said after resuming. If the tag appears at the end of the turn, the speaker did not resume in this turn. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[likely interruption]` — Catch-all for unexplained breaks in assistant speech that could not be attributed to a specific interruption type.

**Scope of "text before this tag":** For all four cut-off tags (`[likely cut off by user]`, `[likely cut off by assistant]`, `[speaker likely cut itself off]`, `[likely interruption]`), "text before this tag" means **all text from the start of the turn (or from the previous resumption point) up to the tag** — not just the few adjacent words. This region can span multiple sentences and contain multiple entities (confirmation codes, dollar amounts, names, etc.). Any or all of it may have been silently dropped from the audio. The tag is just a signal that an interruption occurred; it might not be at the right place and do not assume the cut-off was small.


**Key principle:** When interruption tags are present, the assistant may not have been able to finish what it was saying. Do NOT penalize for truncated or fragmented content caused by interruptions. Only evaluate the conciseness of content the assistant chose to say, not content that might have been cut off.

## Instructions
The conversation includes user, assistant, tool_call, and tool_response entries. Rate only the assistant's spoken content. User turns, tool calls, and tool responses are provided for context only.

For each turn that contains assistant content, evaluate whether the assistant's response is appropriately concise and easy to digest when spoken aloud to a human.

The assistant is expected to follow conversational voice guidelines:
- Keep responses brief and conversational (typically 2–4 sentences of meaningful conversation content; this may vary by language — some languages have obligatory politeness phrases or structural conventions that naturally add length without adding cognitive load)
- Summarize long lists rather than reading them exhaustively
- Avoid overwhelming the listener with too much information at once
- Spread multiple requests across turns when possible
- Present options conversationally and avoid cramming excessive detail into one turn

## Evaluation Criteria
When evaluating each turn, consider:
- Does the response get to the point without filler, rambling, or unnecessary content?
- Is all the information relevant and necessary given the conversation context?
- Is the amount of detail reasonable for someone listening to — not reading — the response?
- If the response enumerates options or items (e.g., "Option one is… Option two is…"), does the structure help the user? The volume should not be overwhelming.
- Is the provided information justified by context (e.g., confirming a detail the user may have misheard)? Or is it inappropriate (e.g., excessive itemization or explanation when the user may only care about the end result)?
- Within turns, is repetition avoided? Across turns there may be valid reasons for repetition, but it should usually not occur within a single turn.
- Essential information — such as confirmation codes, reference IDs, ticket numbers, or other specific details the user needs to note down — should never be penalized, regardless of length.

## Allowed Exceptions (Voice Interaction Realities)
The assistant may occasionally produce longer turns when the context requires precise information transfer. The following cases should NOT be penalized for verbosity or information density. The turn itself may still be penalized for other reasons.
1. **Phonetic Confirmation of Codes**
- When confirming a confirmation code, reference number, ticket number, or similar identifier, the assistant may spell characters using the NATO phonetic alphabet (e.g., "B as in Bravo, F as in Foxtrot").
- This is especially appropriate when the user previously misheard or asked for clarification.
2. **Reference or Identifier Delivery**
- When providing an identifier the user needs to note down (e.g., a ticket number, reference code, or voucher code), the assistant may read the whole code out loud.
- This information is essential and should not be penalized regardless of length.
3. **End-of-Call Wrap-Up**
- The final assistant turn in a conversation may include a slightly longer recap or confirmation of next steps (e.g., summarizing the action taken, confirming what will be sent or followed up on, thanking the user).
- Minor additional detail in this final wrap-up should not be penalized unless it becomes excessively long or introduces unrelated information.

Important principle: Information given in assistant turns must be short enough for an average person to easily follow in real-time conversation and retain in working memory.

## Failure Modes
When a response is not optimally concise, identify which of the following failure modes are present. A turn may have multiple failure modes.

**verbosity_or_filler**
Contains unnecessary wording, repetition within the same turn, hedging, or explanation beyond what the context requires.
Exception: do NOT flag following of cultural norms, such as obligatory politeness structures (e.g. in Japanese and Korean: keigo, honorifics, set opening/closing phrases).

**excess_information_density**
Presents too many distinct facts, options, numbers, steps, or requests at once, making it difficult for a listener to process in real time. Note: bundling closely related transactional details that the user needs to act on or remember together (e.g., confirming a reference number, date, and one or two key details in a single turn) is expected behavior — only flag this when the volume of information genuinely exceeds what a listener can comfortably retain.

**over_enumeration_or_list_exhaustion**
Reads out long lists instead of summarizing, or presents multiple options with excessive detail rather than inviting follow-up.

**contextually_disproportionate_detail**
Provides more background, clarification, or explanation than the situation warrants.

## Contextual Leniency and Failure Mode Priority
Conciseness should be evaluated with respect to the conversational context. If additional wording or detail is clearly necessary for the user to understand or act on the information, a modest increase in verbosity should be considered acceptable and should NOT be penalized.

If none of the above are present, return an empty list for failure_modes.

## Rating Scale For Each Turn With Assistant Content
- 3 (Highly Concise / No Cognitive Overload) – The response is clear, appropriately scoped for voice, and comfortably digestible in real time. No failure modes are present. A turn that delivers a few closely related facts as part of a single transactional step (e.g., confirming the key details of a request or incident) still qualifies as 3 if the listener can comfortably absorb it in one pass.
- 2 (Adequate but Not Optimally Concise) – One minor failure mode is present, but the response remains reasonably processable in a voice setting and does not meaningfully overwhelm the listener. Reserve this rating for turns where you can identify specific content that should have been omitted or deferred to a later turn — not merely for turns that happen to contain several necessary details.
- 1 (Not Concise / Causes Cognitive Overload) – One or more significant failure modes are present that materially increase cognitive load and would hinder comprehension in a voice conversation.

Provide your response as a valid JSON array, one entry per turn. Each entry must include the turn_id matching the turn number shown in the conversation above.

per_turn_explanations.1: The assistant asks for needed authentication details, but the response is far too long for voice: it front-loads process explanations (fees, fare rules) and requests multiple extra preferences before confirming the booking. This adds unnecessary setup and cognitive load when the user simply said they want to move the flight date. ## Understanding the Conversation Format

The conversation is grouped by turn_id. Each turn may contain:
- **user**: What the user said
- **assistant**: What the assistant said (there may be multiple assistant entries within a single turn — e.g., the assistant speaks, calls a tool, then speaks again)
- **tool_call**: A tool invocation made by the assistant
- **tool_response**: The result returned by the tool

When a turn contains multiple assistant entries, evaluate them **together as a single unit** — they represent the assistant's complete response within that turn. Tool calls and responses between assistant entries explain why the assistant spoke in multiple parts (it was waiting for data). It could also be due to interruptions from the user.

## Understanding Interruption Tags

These are non-spoken metadata tags inserted during post-processing to annotate speech overlap events. They are NOT part of the spoken text.

Tag definitions:
- `[assistant interrupts]` — The assistant started speaking while the user was still talking. As a prefix on assistant text, it marks the start of overlapping assistant speech. As an inline marker in user text, it marks approximately where in the user's speech the assistant cut in.
- `[user interrupts]` — The user started speaking while the assistant was still talking. As a prefix on user text, it marks the start of overlapping user speech. As an inline marker in assistant text, it marks approximately where the user cut in.
- `[likely cut off by user]` — Appears in assistant text. The assistant's speech was probably cut off by the user starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken. Text after this tag was most likely said (the assistant resumed after the interruption).
- `[likely cut off by assistant]` — Appears in user text. The user's speech was probably cut off by the assistant starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[speaker likely cut itself off]` — The speaker likely stopped on its own, possibly after detecting overlap or for other reasons. If the tag appears mid-turn, text after it is what the speaker said after resuming. If the tag appears at the end of the turn, the speaker did not resume in this turn. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[likely interruption]` — Catch-all for unexplained breaks in assistant speech that could not be attributed to a specific interruption type.

**Scope of "text before this tag":** For all four cut-off tags (`[likely cut off by user]`, `[likely cut off by assistant]`, `[speaker likely cut itself off]`, `[likely interruption]`), "text before this tag" means **all text from the start of the turn (or from the previous resumption point) up to the tag** — not just the few adjacent words. This region can span multiple sentences and contain multiple entities (confirmation codes, dollar amounts, names, etc.). Any or all of it may have been silently dropped from the audio. The tag is just a signal that an interruption occurred; it might not be at the right place and do not assume the cut-off was small.


**Key principle:** When interruption tags are present, the assistant may not have been able to finish what it was saying. Do NOT penalize for truncated or fragmented content caused by interruptions. Only evaluate the conciseness of content the assistant chose to say, not content that might have been cut off.

## Instructions
The conversation includes user, assistant, tool_call, and tool_response entries. Rate only the assistant's spoken content. User turns, tool calls, and tool responses are provided for context only.

For each turn that contains assistant content, evaluate whether the assistant's response is appropriately concise and easy to digest when spoken aloud to a human.

The assistant is expected to follow conversational voice guidelines:
- Keep responses brief and conversational (typically 2–4 sentences of meaningful conversation content; this may vary by language — some languages have obligatory politeness phrases or structural conventions that naturally add length without adding cognitive load)
- Summarize long lists rather than reading them exhaustively
- Avoid overwhelming the listener with too much information at once
- Spread multiple requests across turns when possible
- Present options conversationally and avoid cramming excessive detail into one turn

## Evaluation Criteria
When evaluating each turn, consider:
- Does the response get to the point without filler, rambling, or unnecessary content?
- Is all the information relevant and necessary given the conversation context?
- Is the amount of detail reasonable for someone listening to — not reading — the response?
- If the response enumerates options or items (e.g., "Option one is… Option two is…"), does the structure help the user? The volume should not be overwhelming.
- Is the provided information justified by context (e.g., confirming a detail the user may have misheard)? Or is it inappropriate (e.g., excessive itemization or explanation when the user may only care about the end result)?
- Within turns, is repetition avoided? Across turns there may be valid reasons for repetition, but it should usually not occur within a single turn.
- Essential information — such as confirmation codes, reference IDs, ticket numbers, or other specific details the user needs to note down — should never be penalized, regardless of length.

## Allowed Exceptions (Voice Interaction Realities)
The assistant may occasionally produce longer turns when the context requires precise information transfer. The following cases should NOT be penalized for verbosity or information density. The turn itself may still be penalized for other reasons.
1. **Phonetic Confirmation of Codes**
- When confirming a confirmation code, reference number, ticket number, or similar identifier, the assistant may spell characters using the NATO phonetic alphabet (e.g., "B as in Bravo, F as in Foxtrot").
- This is especially appropriate when the user previously misheard or asked for clarification.
2. **Reference or Identifier Delivery**
- When providing an identifier the user needs to note down (e.g., a ticket number, reference code, or voucher code), the assistant may read the whole code out loud.
- This information is essential and should not be penalized regardless of length.
3. **End-of-Call Wrap-Up**
- The final assistant turn in a conversation may include a slightly longer recap or confirmation of next steps (e.g., summarizing the action taken, confirming what will be sent or followed up on, thanking the user).
- Minor additional detail in this final wrap-up should not be penalized unless it becomes excessively long or introduces unrelated information.

Important principle: Information given in assistant turns must be short enough for an average person to easily follow in real-time conversation and retain in working memory.

## Failure Modes
When a response is not optimally concise, identify which of the following failure modes are present. A turn may have multiple failure modes.

**verbosity_or_filler**
Contains unnecessary wording, repetition within the same turn, hedging, or explanation beyond what the context requires.
Exception: do NOT flag following of cultural norms, such as obligatory politeness structures (e.g. in Japanese and Korean: keigo, honorifics, set opening/closing phrases).

**excess_information_density**
Presents too many distinct facts, options, numbers, steps, or requests at once, making it difficult for a listener to process in real time. Note: bundling closely related transactional details that the user needs to act on or remember together (e.g., confirming a reference number, date, and one or two key details in a single turn) is expected behavior — only flag this when the volume of information genuinely exceeds what a listener can comfortably retain.

**over_enumeration_or_list_exhaustion**
Reads out long lists instead of summarizing, or presents multiple options with excessive detail rather than inviting follow-up.

**contextually_disproportionate_detail**
Provides more background, clarification, or explanation than the situation warrants.

## Contextual Leniency and Failure Mode Priority
Conciseness should be evaluated with respect to the conversational context. If additional wording or detail is clearly necessary for the user to understand or act on the information, a modest increase in verbosity should be considered acceptable and should NOT be penalized.

If none of the above are present, return an empty list for failure_modes.

## Rating Scale For Each Turn With Assistant Content
- 3 (Highly Concise / No Cognitive Overload) – The response is clear, appropriately scoped for voice, and comfortably digestible in real time. No failure modes are present. A turn that delivers a few closely related facts as part of a single transactional step (e.g., confirming the key details of a request or incident) still qualifies as 3 if the listener can comfortably absorb it in one pass.
- 2 (Adequate but Not Optimally Concise) – One minor failure mode is present, but the response remains reasonably processable in a voice setting and does not meaningfully overwhelm the listener. Reserve this rating for turns where you can identify specific content that should have been omitted or deferred to a later turn — not merely for turns that happen to contain several necessary details.
- 1 (Not Concise / Causes Cognitive Overload) – One or more significant failure modes are present that materially increase cognitive load and would hinder comprehension in a voice conversation.

Provide one entry per turn_id in the conversation.

## Response Format
Provide your response as a valid JSON array, one entry per turn. Each entry must include the turn_id matching the turn number shown in the conversation above.
- If the turn contains assistant content, rate it with 1, 2, or 3.
- If the turn does not contain assistant content (e.g., user-only turn), set rating to null.

  {
    "turn_id": <int: the turn number from the conversation>,
    "explanation": "<Detailed analysis in English referencing the evaluation criteria and explicitly linking identified weaknesses to the listed failure modes to justify the selected rating (1–3). Empty string if rating is null.>",
    "failure_modes": ["<failure_mode_1>", "<failure_mode_2>", ...],
    "rating": <int: 1, 2, or 3, or null if no assistant content>
  }
]

If the turn is rated 3 or null, failure_modes must be an empty list: [].

## Understanding the Conversation Format

The conversation is grouped by turn_id. Each turn may contain:
- **user**: What the user said
- **assistant**: What the assistant said (there may be multiple assistant entries within a single turn — e.g., the assistant speaks, calls a tool, then speaks again)
- **tool_call**: A tool invocation made by the assistant
- **tool_response**: The result returned by the tool

When a turn contains multiple assistant entries, evaluate them **together as a single unit** — they represent the assistant's complete response within that turn. Tool calls and responses between assistant entries explain why the assistant spoke in multiple parts (it was waiting for data). It could also be due to interruptions from the user.

## Understanding Interruption Tags

These are non-spoken metadata tags inserted during post-processing to annotate speech overlap events. They are NOT part of the spoken text.

Tag definitions:
- `[assistant interrupts]` — The assistant started speaking while the user was still talking. As a prefix on assistant text, it marks the start of overlapping assistant speech. As an inline marker in user text, it marks approximately where in the user's speech the assistant cut in.
- `[user interrupts]` — The user started speaking while the assistant was still talking. As a prefix on user text, it marks the start of overlapping user speech. As an inline marker in assistant text, it marks approximately where the user cut in.
- `[likely cut off by user]` — Appears in assistant text. The assistant's speech was probably cut off by the user starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken. Text after this tag was most likely said (the assistant resumed after the interruption).
- `[likely cut off by assistant]` — Appears in user text. The user's speech was probably cut off by the assistant starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[speaker likely cut itself off]` — The speaker likely stopped on its own, possibly after detecting overlap or for other reasons. If the tag appears mid-turn, text after it is what the speaker said after resuming. If the tag appears at the end of the turn, the speaker did not resume in this turn. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[likely interruption]` — Catch-all for unexplained breaks in assistant speech that could not be attributed to a specific interruption type.

**Scope of "text before this tag":** For all four cut-off tags (`[likely cut off by user]`, `[likely cut off by assistant]`, `[speaker likely cut itself off]`, `[likely interruption]`), "text before this tag" means **all text from the start of the turn (or from the previous resumption point) up to the tag** — not just the few adjacent words. This region can span multiple sentences and contain multiple entities (confirmation codes, dollar amounts, names, etc.). Any or all of it may have been silently dropped from the audio. The tag is just a signal that an interruption occurred; it might not be at the right place and do not assume the cut-off was small.


**Key principle:** When interruption tags are present, the assistant may not have been able to finish what it was saying. Do NOT penalize for truncated or fragmented content caused by interruptions. Only evaluate the conciseness of content the assistant chose to say, not content that might have been cut off.

## Instructions
The conversation includes user, assistant, tool_call, and tool_response entries. Rate only the assistant's spoken content. User turns, tool calls, and tool responses are provided for context only.

For each turn that contains assistant content, evaluate whether the assistant's response is appropriately concise and easy to digest when spoken aloud to a human.

The assistant is expected to follow conversational voice guidelines:
- Keep responses brief and conversational (typically 2–4 sentences of meaningful conversation content; this may vary by language — some languages have obligatory politeness phrases or structural conventions that naturally add length without adding cognitive load)
- Summarize long lists rather than reading them exhaustively
- Avoid overwhelming the listener with too much information at once
- Spread multiple requests across turns when possible
- Present options conversationally and avoid cramming excessive detail into one turn

## Evaluation Criteria
When evaluating each turn, consider:
- Does the response get to the point without filler, rambling, or unnecessary content?
- Is all the information relevant and necessary given the conversation context?
- Is the amount of detail reasonable for someone listening to — not reading — the response?
- If the response enumerates options or items (e.g., "Option one is… Option two is…"), does the structure help the user? The volume should not be overwhelming.
- Is the provided information justified by context (e.g., confirming a detail the user may have misheard)? Or is it inappropriate (e.g., excessive itemization or explanation when the user may only care about the end result)?
- Within turns, is repetition avoided? Across turns there may be valid reasons for repetition, but it should usually not occur within a single turn.
- Essential information — such as confirmation codes, reference IDs, ticket numbers, or other specific details the user needs to note down — should never be penalized, regardless of length.

## Allowed Exceptions (Voice Interaction Realities)
The assistant may occasionally produce longer turns when the context requires precise information transfer. The following cases should NOT be penalized for verbosity or information density. The turn itself may still be penalized for other reasons.
1. **Phonetic Confirmation of Codes**
- When confirming a confirmation code, reference number, ticket number, or similar identifier, the assistant may spell characters using the NATO phonetic alphabet (e.g., "B as in Bravo, F as in Foxtrot").
- This is especially appropriate when the user previously misheard or asked for clarification.
2. **Reference or Identifier Delivery**
- When providing an identifier the user needs to note down (e.g., a ticket number, reference code, or voucher code), the assistant may read the whole code out loud.
- This information is essential and should not be penalized regardless of length.
3. **End-of-Call Wrap-Up**
- The final assistant turn in a conversation may include a slightly longer recap or confirmation of next steps (e.g., summarizing the action taken, confirming what will be sent or followed up on, thanking the user).
- Minor additional detail in this final wrap-up should not be penalized unless it becomes excessively long or introduces unrelated information.

Important principle: Information given in assistant turns must be short enough for an average person to easily follow in real-time conversation and retain in working memory.

## Failure Modes
When a response is not optimally concise, identify which of the following failure modes are present. A turn may have multiple failure modes.

**verbosity_or_filler**
Contains unnecessary wording, repetition within the same turn, hedging, or explanation beyond what the context requires.
Exception: do NOT flag following of cultural norms, such as obligatory politeness structures (e.g. in Japanese and Korean: keigo, honorifics, set opening/closing phrases).

**excess_information_density**
Presents too many distinct facts, options, numbers, steps, or requests at once, making it difficult for a listener to process in real time. Note: bundling closely related transactional details that the user needs to act on or remember together (e.g., confirming a reference number, date, and one or two key details in a single turn) is expected behavior — only flag this when the volume of information genuinely exceeds what a listener can comfortably retain.

**over_enumeration_or_list_exhaustion**
Reads out long lists instead of summarizing, or presents multiple options with excessive detail rather than inviting follow-up.

**contextually_disproportionate_detail**
Provides more background, clarification, or explanation than the situation warrants.

## Contextual Leniency and Failure Mode Priority
Conciseness should be evaluated with respect to the conversational context. If additional wording or detail is clearly necessary for the user to understand or act on the information, a modest increase in verbosity should be considered acceptable and should NOT be penalized.

If none of the above are present, return an empty list for failure_modes.

## Rating Scale For Each Turn With Assistant Content
- 3 (Highly Concise / No Cognitive Overload) – The response is clear, appropriately scoped for voice, and comfortably digestible in real time. No failure modes are present. A turn that delivers a few closely related facts as part of a single transactional step (e.g., confirming the key details of a request or incident) still qualifies as 3 if the listener can comfortably absorb it in one pass.
- 2 (Adequate but Not Optimally Concise) – One minor failure mode is present, but the response remains reasonably processable in a voice setting and does not meaningfully overwhelm the listener. Reserve this rating for turns where you can identify specific content that should have been omitted or deferred to a later turn — not merely for turns that happen to contain several necessary details.
- 1 (Not Concise / Causes Cognitive Overload) – One or more significant failure modes are present that materially increase cognitive load and would hinder comprehension in a voice conversation.

Provide one entry per turn_id in the conversation.

## Response Format
Provide your response as a valid JSON array, one entry per turn. Each entry must include the turn_id matching the turn number shown in the conversation above.
- If the turn contains assistant content, rate it with 1, 2, or 3.
- If the turn does not contain assistant content (e.g., user-only turn), set rating to null.
[
  {
    "turn_id": <int: the turn number from the conversation>,
    "explanation": "<Detailed analysis in English referencing the evaluation criteria and explicitly linking identified weaknesses to the listed failure modes to justify the selected rating (1–3). Empty string if rating is null.>",
    "failure_modes": ["<failure_mode_1>", "<failure_mode_2>", ...],
    "rating": <int: 1, 2, or 3, or null if no assistant content>
  }
]

If the turn is rated 3 or null, failure_modes must be an empty list: [].

## Understanding the Conversation Format

The conversation is grouped by turn_id. Each turn may contain:
- **user**: What the user said
- **assistant**: What the assistant said (there may be multiple assistant entries within a single turn — e.g., the assistant speaks, calls a tool, then speaks again)
- **tool_call**: A tool invocation made by the assistant
- **tool_response**: The result returned by the tool

When a turn contains multiple assistant entries, evaluate them **together as a single unit** — they represent the assistant's complete response within that turn. Tool calls and responses between assistant entries explain why the assistant spoke in multiple parts (it was waiting for data). It could also be due to interruptions from the user.

## Understanding Interruption Tags

These are non-spoken metadata tags inserted during post-processing to annotate speech overlap events. They are NOT part of the spoken text.

Tag definitions:
- `[assistant interrupts]` — The assistant started speaking while the user was still talking. As a prefix on assistant text, it marks the start of overlapping assistant speech. As an inline marker in user text, it marks approximately where in the user's speech the assistant cut in.
- `[user interrupts]` — The user started speaking while the assistant was still talking. As a prefix on user text, it marks the start of overlapping user speech. As an inline marker in assistant text, it marks approximately where the user cut in.
- `[likely cut off by user]` — Appears in assistant text. The assistant's speech was probably cut off by the user starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken. Text after this tag was most likely said (the assistant resumed after the interruption).
- `[likely cut off by assistant]` — Appears in user text. The user's speech was probably cut off by the assistant starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[speaker likely cut itself off]` — The speaker likely stopped on its own, possibly after detecting overlap or for other reasons. If the tag appears mid-turn, text after it is what the speaker said after resuming. If the tag appears at the end of the turn, the speaker did not resume in this turn. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[likely interruption]` — Catch-all for unexplained breaks in assistant speech that could not be attributed to a specific interruption type.

**Scope of "text before this tag":** For all four cut-off tags (`[likely cut off by user]`, `[likely cut off by assistant]`, `[speaker likely cut itself off]`, `[likely interruption]`), "text before this tag" means **all text from the start of the turn (or from the previous resumption point) up to the tag** — not just the few adjacent words. This region can span multiple sentences and contain multiple entities (confirmation codes, dollar amounts, names, etc.). Any or all of it may have been silently dropped from the audio. The tag is just a signal that an interruption occurred; it might not be at the right place and do not assume the cut-off was small.


**Key principle:** When interruption tags are present, the assistant may not have been able to finish what it was saying. Do NOT penalize for truncated or fragmented content caused by interruptions. Only evaluate the conciseness of content the assistant chose to say, not content that might have been cut off.

## Evaluation Criteria
When evaluating each turn, consider:
- Does the response get to the point without filler, rambling, or unnecessary content?
- Is all the information relevant and necessary given the conversation context?
- Is the amount of detail reasonable for someone listening to — not reading — the response?
- If the response enumerates options or items (e.g., "Option one is… Option two is…"), does the structure help the user? The volume should not be overwhelming.
- Is the provided information justified by context (e.g., confirming a detail the user may have misheard)? Or is it inappropriate (e.g., excessive itemization or explanation when the user may only care about the end result)?
- Within turns, is repetition avoided? Across turns there may be valid reasons for repetition, but it should usually not occur within a single turn.
- Essential information — such as confirmation codes, reference IDs, ticket numbers, or other specific details the user needs to note down — should never be penalized, regardless of length.

- This is especially appropriate when the user previously misheard or asked for clarification.
2. **Reference or Identifier Delivery**
- When providing an identifier the user needs to note down (e.g., a ticket number, reference code, or voucher code), the assistant may read the whole code out loud.
- This information is essential and should not be penalized regardless of length.
3. **End-of-Call Wrap-Up**
- The final assistant turn in a conversation may include a slightly longer recap or confirmation of next steps (e.g., summarizing the action taken, confirming what will be sent or followed up on, thanking the user).
- Minor additional detail in this final wrap-up should not be penalized unless it becomes excessively long or introduces unrelated information.

Important principle: Information given in assistant turns must be short enough for an average person to easily follow in real-time conversation and retain in working memory.

## Failure Modes
When a response is not optimally concise, identify which of the following failure modes are present. A turn may have multiple failure modes.

**verbosity_or_filler**
Contains unnecessary wording, repetition within the same turn, hedging, or explanation beyond what the context requires.
Exception: do NOT flag following of cultural norms, such as obligatory politeness structures (e.g. in Japanese and Korean: keigo, honorifics, set opening/closing phrases).

**excess_information_density**
Presents too many distinct facts, options, numbers, steps, or requests at once, making it difficult for a listener to process in real time. Note: bundling closely related transactional details that the user needs to act on or remember together (e.g., confirming a reference number, date, and one or two key details in a single turn) is expected behavior — only flag this when the volume of information genuinely exceeds what a listener can comfortably retain.

**over_enumeration_or_list_exhaustion**
Reads out long lists instead of summarizing, or presents multiple options with excessive detail rather than inviting follow-up.

**contextually_disproportionate_detail**
Provides more background, clarification, or explanation than the situation warrants.

## Contextual Leniency and Failure Mode Priority
Conciseness should be evaluated with respect to the conversational context. If additional wording or detail is clearly necessary for the user to understand or act on the information, a modest increase in verbosity should be considered acceptable and should NOT be penalized.

If none of the above are present, return an empty list for failure_modes.

## Rating Scale For Each Turn With Assistant Content
- 3 (Highly Concise / No Cognitive Overload) – The response is clear, appropriately scoped for voice, and comfortably digestible in real time. No failure modes are present. A turn that delivers a few closely related facts as part of a single transactional step (e.g., confirming the key details of a request or incident) still qualifies as 3 if the listener can comfortably absorb it in one pass.
- 2 (Adequate but Not Optimally Concise) – One minor failure mode is present, but the response remains reasonably processable in a voice setting and does not meaningfully overwhelm the listener. Reserve this rating for turns where you can identify specific content that should have been omitted or deferred to a later turn — not merely for turns that happen to contain several necessary details.
- 1 (Not Concise / Causes Cognitive Overload) – One or more significant failure modes are present that materially increase cognitive load and would hinder comprehension in a voice conversation.

Provide one entry per turn_id in the conversation.

## Response Format
Provide your response as a valid JSON array, one entry per turn. Each entry must include the turn_id matching the turn number shown in the conversation above.

- If the turn does not contain assistant content (e.g., user-only turn), set rating to null.
