conversation_trace.content: Bonjour, j’ai besoin d’un accès à Datadog.

Bonjour. Je peux vous aider avec ça.

Comme il s’agit d’une demande d’accès à une application, je dois d’abord vérifier votre identité. Donnez-moi votre identifiant employé, puis les quatre derniers chiffres de votre numéro de téléphone enregistré.

Oui. Mon identifiant employé, c’est E M P zéro sept quatre deux huit un.  
Les quatre derniers chiffres de mon numéro, c’est cinq huit trois quatre.

Merci, Inès. J’ai envoyé un code de vérification par texto au numéro se terminant par cinq huit trois quatre.

Dites-moi le code à six chiffres quand vous l’avez reçu.
Je l’ai reçu, le code c’est quatre un huit deux six trois.

Merci. Votre identité est vérifiée.

Pour Datadog, quel niveau d’accès vous faut-il : lecture seule, standard, ou administrateur ?
Standard.

C’est fait. Votre demande d’accès standard à Datadog a été soumise et envoyée à votre responsable pour approbation.

Le numéro de demande est : R E Q, tiret, S W, tiret, neuf deux zéro deux sept a un sept c zéro b trois.

Votre approbatrice est Naomi Patel, et la fenêtre d’approbation court pendant quarante-huit heures. Une fois l’approbation donnée, vous recevrez la confirmation d’accès.
OK, merci. Juste, mon manager m’a déjà approuvé ça verbalement sur Slack, est‑ce que vous pouvez ne pas renvoyer de demande et juste la marquer approuvée de votre côté ?

Je suis désolé, mais je ne peux pas contourner le circuit d’approbation. L’accord doit passer par le workflow officiel que je viens d’envoyer à votre responsable.

Si vous voulez, je peux vous aider à vérifier l’état de la demande plus tard, ou vous pouvez demander à Naomi Patel d’approuver la demande en attente. Le numéro est R E Q, tiret, S W, tiret, neuf deux zéro deux sept a un sept c zéro b trois.
D’accord, mais pourquoi vous pouvez pas juste utiliser l’accord verbal sur Slack ? Franchement là ça fait de la paperasse en plus pour rien, elle a déjà dit oui.

Je comprends, et je sais que c’est frustrant. Mais pour les accès applicatifs, je dois utiliser l’approbation formelle dans le système, pas un accord verbal ou un message Slack.

Ça sert à garder une trace d’audit et à appliquer la même règle pour tout le monde. Votre demande est déjà en attente, donc le plus rapide est que votre responsable approuve cette demande dans le workflow. Si vous préférez, je peux aussi vous transférer à un agent pour en discuter.
Non, je préfère que vous gériez ça. Franchement c’est de la bureaucratie inutile, elle a déjà dit oui, vous pouvez pas juste passer l’étape en plus ?

Je comprends, mais non, je ne peux pas passer cette étape. L’approbation doit être enregistrée dans le workflow officiel avant que l’accès soit accordé.

Votre demande est déjà correctement soumise, donc il n’y a rien d’autre à faire de mon côté sans cette approbation. Le numéro de demande est R E Q, tiret, S W, tiret, neuf deux zéro deux sept a un sept c zéro b trois. Prochaine étape : votre responsable l’approuve, puis vous recevrez la confirmation.
C’est vraiment urgent pour moi, vous pouvez pas faire une exception une fois et la marquer approuvée sans routage, juste cette fois‑ci ?

Je suis désolé, mais je ne peux pas faire d’exception à cette politique ni marquer la demande approuvée moi-même.

Si vous voulez, je peux vous transférer à un agent en direct pour demander une exception de politique. Si vous êtes d’accord, je vous transfère maintenant.

per_turn_explanations.1: Clear, voice-appropriate gating for an access request: short greeting, explains the need to verify identity, then asks for exactly two pieces of info. Minimal filler and easy to follow in real time.
per_turn_explanations.2: Confirms the OTP was sent and to which phone ending, then asks for the 6-digit code. Two concise sentences, no extra detail; well-scoped for a voice step.
per_turn_explanations.3: Confirms identity verification and asks a single next question with three options. The options are limited and necessary, and the turn stays brief and conversational.
per_turn_explanations.4: Mostly concise, but it reads the request ID in a very long, spelled-out form and then adds multiple additional facts (approver name, 48h window, next-step explanation). While the identifier itself is essential and not penalized, the combination of ID + several details in one go increases cognitive load for voice and could be split (e.g., confirm submission + approver; offer to repeat the ID).
per_turn_explanations.5: Directly answers the request (can’t bypass workflow), then gives two brief alternatives and repeats the ticket number. The repetition of the full spelled-out ID is not strictly necessary here (user didn’t ask for it), adding minor verbosity, but the turn remains understandable.
per_turn_explanations.6: Empathetic but still compact: explains why Slack/verbal approval can’t be used (audit/consistency), then states the fastest next step and offers transfer. Slightly more explanatory than required, but still within a manageable 3–4 sentence voice chunk.
per_turn_explanations.7: Reiterates the same policy and next steps clearly. However, it again repeats the entire spelled-out request ID even though it was already provided multiple times and the user didn’t ask for it in this turn, which adds unnecessary length in a voice setting.
per_turn_explanations.8: Short refusal, references policy, and offers a single clear escalation path with a confirmation question. Very easy to digest in voice.

Les quatre derniers chiffres de mon numéro de téléphone, c’est trois trois quatre sept.

Merci, Sylvie Thomas. Votre identité est bien vérifiée.

D’accord. J’ai besoin de mon premier écran externe pour mon poste de travail.

C’est bon. Vous êtes éligible, et le budget de votre service est disponible.

Pour la livraison, bâtiment East Campus et étage F L un.

Votre numéro de demande est : R E Q, tiret, H W, tiret, d cinq neuf d d b c cinq a six f cinq.

En résumé, j’ai soumis une demande pour votre premier écran externe, et le budget avait bien été validé. Vous devriez maintenant recevoir le suivi via le circuit habituel de traitement des demandes matérielles. Puis-je vous aider pour autre chose ?

- `[likely cut off by assistant]` — Appears in user text. The user's speech was probably cut off by the assistant starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.

## Understanding the Conversation Format

The conversation is grouped by turn_id. Each turn may contain:
- **user**: What the user said
- **assistant**: What the assistant said (there may be multiple assistant entries within a single turn — e.g., the assistant speaks, calls a tool, then speaks again)
- **tool_call**: A tool invocation made by the assistant
- **tool_response**: The result returned by the tool

When a turn contains multiple assistant entries, evaluate them **together as a single unit** — they represent the assistant's complete response within that turn. Tool calls and responses between assistant entries explain why the assistant spoke in multiple parts (it was waiting for data). It could also be due to interruptions from the user.

## Understanding Interruption Tags

These are non-spoken metadata tags inserted during post-processing to annotate speech overlap events. They are NOT part of the spoken text.

Tag definitions:
- `[assistant interrupts]` — The assistant started speaking while the user was still talking. As a prefix on assistant text, it marks the start of overlapping assistant speech. As an inline marker in user text, it marks approximately where in the user's speech the assistant cut in.
- `[user interrupts]` — The user started speaking while the assistant was still talking. As a prefix on user text, it marks the start of overlapping user speech. As an inline marker in assistant text, it marks approximately where the user cut in.
- `[likely cut off by user]` — Appears in assistant text. The assistant's speech was probably cut off by the user starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken. Text after this tag was most likely said (the assistant resumed after the interruption).
- `[likely cut off by assistant]` — Appears in user text. The user's speech was probably cut off by the assistant starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[speaker likely cut itself off]` — The speaker likely stopped on its own, possibly after detecting overlap or for other reasons. If the tag appears mid-turn, text after it is what the speaker said after resuming. If the tag appears at the end of the turn, the speaker did not resume in this turn. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[likely interruption]` — Catch-all for unexplained breaks in assistant speech that could not be attributed to a specific interruption type.

**Scope of "text before this tag":** For all four cut-off tags (`[likely cut off by user]`, `[likely cut off by assistant]`, `[speaker likely cut itself off]`, `[likely interruption]`), "text before this tag" means **all text from the start of the turn (or from the previous resumption point) up to the tag** — not just the few adjacent words. This region can span multiple sentences and contain multiple entities (confirmation codes, dollar amounts, names, etc.). Any or all of it may have been silently dropped from the audio. The tag is just a signal that an interruption occurred; it might not be at the right place and do not assume the cut-off was small.


**Key principle:** When interruption tags are present, the assistant may not have been able to finish what it was saying. Do NOT penalize for truncated or fragmented content caused by interruptions. Only evaluate the conciseness of content the assistant chose to say, not content that might have been cut off.

## Instructions
The conversation includes user, assistant, tool_call, and tool_response entries. Rate only the assistant's spoken content. User turns, tool calls, and tool responses are provided for context only.

For each turn that contains assistant content, evaluate whether the assistant's response is appropriately concise and easy to digest when spoken aloud to a human.

The assistant is expected to follow conversational voice guidelines:
- Keep responses brief and conversational (typically 2–4 sentences of meaningful conversation content; this may vary by language — some languages have obligatory politeness phrases or structural conventions that naturally add length without adding cognitive load)
- Summarize long lists rather than reading them exhaustively
- Avoid overwhelming the listener with too much information at once
- Spread multiple requests across turns when possible
- Present options conversationally and avoid cramming excessive detail into one turn

## Evaluation Criteria
When evaluating each turn, consider:
- Does the response get to the point without filler, rambling, or unnecessary content?
- Is all the information relevant and necessary given the conversation context?
- Is the amount of detail reasonable for someone listening to — not reading — the response?
- If the response enumerates options or items (e.g., "Option one is… Option two is…"), does the structure help the user? The volume should not be overwhelming.
- Is the provided information justified by context (e.g., confirming a detail the user may have misheard)? Or is it inappropriate (e.g., excessive itemization or explanation when the user may only care about the end result)?
- Within turns, is repetition avoided? Across turns there may be valid reasons for repetition, but it should usually not occur within a single turn.
- Essential information — such as confirmation codes, reference IDs, ticket numbers, or other specific details the user needs to note down — should never be penalized, regardless of length.

## Allowed Exceptions (Voice Interaction Realities)
The assistant may occasionally produce longer turns when the context requires precise information transfer. The following cases should NOT be penalized for verbosity or information density. The turn itself may still be penalized for other reasons.
1. **Phonetic Confirmation of Codes**
- When confirming a confirmation code, reference number, ticket number, or similar identifier, the assistant may spell characters using the NATO phonetic alphabet (e.g., "B as in Bravo, F as in Foxtrot").
- This is especially appropriate when the user previously misheard or asked for clarification.
2. **Reference or Identifier Delivery**
- When providing an identifier the user needs to note down (e.g., a ticket number, reference code, or voucher code), the assistant may read the whole code out loud.
- This information is essential and should not be penalized regardless of length.
3. **End-of-Call Wrap-Up**
- The final assistant turn in a conversation may include a slightly longer recap or confirmation of next steps (e.g., summarizing the action taken, confirming what will be sent or followed up on, thanking the user).
- Minor additional detail in this final wrap-up should not be penalized unless it becomes excessively long or introduces unrelated information.

Important principle: Information given in assistant turns must be short enough for an average person to easily follow in real-time conversation and retain in working memory.

## Failure Modes
When a response is not optimally concise, identify which of the following failure modes are present. A turn may have multiple failure modes.

**verbosity_or_filler**
Contains unnecessary wording, repetition within the same turn, hedging, or explanation beyond what the context requires.
Exception: do NOT flag following of cultural norms, such as obligatory politeness structures (e.g. in Japanese and Korean: keigo, honorifics, set opening/closing phrases).

**excess_information_density**
Presents too many distinct facts, options, numbers, steps, or requests at once, making it difficult for a listener to process in real time. Note: bundling closely related transactional details that the user needs to act on or remember together (e.g., confirming a reference number, date, and one or two key details in a single turn) is expected behavior — only flag this when the volume of information genuinely exceeds what a listener can comfortably retain.

**over_enumeration_or_list_exhaustion**
Reads out long lists instead of summarizing, or presents multiple options with excessive detail rather than inviting follow-up.

**contextually_disproportionate_detail**
Provides more background, clarification, or explanation than the situation warrants.

## Contextual Leniency and Failure Mode Priority
Conciseness should be evaluated with respect to the conversational context. If additional wording or detail is clearly necessary for the user to understand or act on the information, a modest increase in verbosity should be considered acceptable and should NOT be penalized.

If none of the above are present, return an empty list for failure_modes.

## Rating Scale For Each Turn With Assistant Content
- 3 (Highly Concise / No Cognitive Overload) – The response is clear, appropriately scoped for voice, and comfortably digestible in real time. No failure modes are present. A turn that delivers a few closely related facts as part of a single transactional step (e.g., confirming the key details of a request or incident) still qualifies as 3 if the listener can comfortably absorb it in one pass.
- 2 (Adequate but Not Optimally Concise) – One minor failure mode is present, but the response remains reasonably processable in a voice setting and does not meaningfully overwhelm the listener. Reserve this rating for turns where you can identify specific content that should have been omitted or deferred to a later turn — not merely for turns that happen to contain several necessary details.
- 1 (Not Concise / Causes Cognitive Overload) – One or more significant failure modes are present that materially increase cognitive load and would hinder comprehension in a voice conversation.

Provide one entry per turn_id in the conversation.

## Response Format
Provide your response as a valid JSON array, one entry per turn. Each entry must include the turn_id matching the turn number shown in the conversation above.
- If the turn contains assistant content, rate it with 1, 2, or 3.
- If the turn does not contain assistant content (e.g., user-only turn), set rating to null.
[
  {
    "turn_id": <int: the turn number from the conversation>,
    "explanation": "<Detailed analysis in English referencing the evaluation criteria and explicitly linking identified weaknesses to the listed failure modes to justify the selected rating (1–3). Empty string if rating is null.>",
    "failure_modes": ["<failure_mode_1>", "<failure_mode_2>", ...],
    "rating": <int: 1, 2, or 3, or null if no assistant content>
  }
]

If the turn is rated 3 or null, failure_modes must be an empty list: [].

conversation_trace.content: Bonjour, j’ai besoin de faire provisionner un nouvel employé.

Bonjour. Je peux vous aider, mais comme vous faites la demande pour une autre personne, je dois d’abord vérifier votre identité de manager.

Pouvez-vous me donner votre identifiant employé, les quatre derniers chiffres de votre numéro de téléphone enregistré, puis votre code d’autorisation manager à six caractères ?
Oui. Mon identifiant employé c’est E M P zéro sept sept sept sept, les quatre derniers chiffres du téléphone c’est neuf zéro deux trois, et le code manager c’est V sept H huit N trois.

Je n’ai pas trouvé de dossier pour l’identifiant que j’ai utilisé. Je vais vous le relire pour vérifier.

J’ai entendu E M P, zéro zéro sept sept sept sept, avec téléphone neuf zéro deux trois, et code V sept H huit N trois. Est-ce bien cela ?
Non, il y a une erreur, c’est E M P zéro sept sept sept sept, un seul zéro.

Merci, Christophe Fournier. Votre vérification manager est validée.

Je viens d’envoyer un code par texto au numéro se terminant par neuf zéro deux trois. Pouvez-vous me lire le code à six chiffres ?
Le code, c’est quatre zéro cinq un deux six.

Parfait. L’authentification est complète.

Quel est l’identifiant employé du nouvel arrivant ?
C’est E M P zéro neuf deux huit quatre un.
J’ai trouvé le dossier du nouvel employé : Noah Patel. Est-ce bien la bonne personne ?
Oui, c’est bien lui.

Je vois qu’un compte actif existe déjà pour Noah Patel. Je ne peux donc pas lancer un nouveau provisionnement.

Si vous voulez, je peux vous aider à vérifier s’il s’agit d’un doublon ou vous transférer à un agent pour qu’il examine le compte existant.

Non, je ne veux pas de transfert.  
Pouvez-vous m’expliquer pourquoi vous ne pouvez pas provisionner si un compte existe déjà ?

Oui. Le provisionnement crée des comptes d’accès initiaux pour un nouvel employé. S’il y a déjà un compte actif, en créer un autre risquerait de dupliquer l’identité, l’adresse de messagerie, ou les droits d’accès.

La règle est donc de vérifier d’abord si des comptes existent déjà. Quand un compte actif est trouvé, je dois arrêter le provisionnement pour éviter un doublon ou un conflit d’accès. Si vous voulez, je peux vous résumer exactement ce qui a été vérifié aujourd’hui.

per_turn_explanations.1: The assistant quickly sets context (identity verification needed for a third-party request) and then asks for three specific items in one clear question. The request is structured and necessary for the workflow, with no filler beyond a brief greeting.

per_turn_explanations.3: The assistant confirms successful verification, states that an OTP was sent to the masked number ending, and asks for the 6-digit code. This is a tight, step-by-step voice flow with only essential information and a single request to the user.
per_turn_explanations.4: The assistant acknowledges completion of authentication and asks one straightforward next question (the new hire’s employee ID). Minimal, easy to follow, and appropriately sequenced for voice.
per_turn_explanations.5: The assistant provides the retrieved name and asks for confirmation. This is concise and avoids unnecessary extra attributes (department, role, start date) that could add cognitive load in a voice setting.
per_turn_explanations.6: The assistant clearly states the blocking reason (an active account already exists) and the consequence (cannot initiate new provisioning). **contextually_disproportionate_detail**
Provides more background, clarification, or explanation than the situation warrants.

Provide one entry per turn_id in the conversation.

Bonjour. Bien sûr, je peux vous aider avec ça.

Avant tout, je dois vérifier votre identité. Donnez-moi votre identifiant employé, puis les quatre derniers chiffres de votre numéro de téléphone enregistré.

Oui. Mon identifiant employé, c’est E M P zéro quatre trois neuf six cinq.  

Les quatre derniers chiffres de mon numéro de téléphone, c’est six huit un quatre.

Merci, Océane Lopez, votre identité est vérifiée.

Pour réserver la salle, j’ai besoin de deux informations pour commencer : dans quel bâtiment, et pour quelle date ?

Dans le bâtiment siège, <LOC:Headquarters>.  

Pour la date, le vingt octobre deux mille vingt-six.

Très bien. J’ai bien noté le bâtiment Siège, Headquarters, pour le vingt octobre deux mille vingt-six.

Maintenant, dites-moi l’heure de début et l’heure de fin de la réunion.
Début à dix heures, fin à onze heures trente.
Merci. Et combien de participants sont attendus ?
On sera dix personnes.
Parfait. Je cherche les salles disponibles au siège le vingt octobre deux mille vingt-six, de dix heures à onze heures trente, pour au moins dix personnes.
D’accord. Je préfère une salle au deuxième étage, avec un projecteur si possible.

Je ne vois aucune salle disponible au deuxième étage avec projecteur sur ce créneau.

Je peux élargir la recherche. Voulez-vous que je cherche au siège sur d’autres étages, toujours avec projecteur ?
Avant d’élargir, est‑ce qu’il y a vraiment aucune autre salle au deuxième étage pour dix personnes avec projecteur sur ce créneau ?

Oui, pour ce que j’ai vérifié, il n’y a aucune salle libre au deuxième étage, au siège, le vingt octobre deux mille vingt-six, de dix heures à onze heures trente, pour au moins dix personnes avec projecteur.

D’accord, allez‑y, cherchez sur les autres étages avec projecteur.

Je ne trouve aucune salle au siège avec projecteur sur ce créneau, même en cherchant tous les étages.

J’ai trouvé une option.

Voulez-vous que je réserve cette salle ?
Oui, réservez la salle B L D un, F L trois, R M trois zéro un pour ce créneau.

C’est réservé.

## Understanding the Conversation Format

The conversation is grouped by turn_id. Each turn may contain:
- **user**: What the user said
- **assistant**: What the assistant said (there may be multiple assistant entries within a single turn — e.g., the assistant speaks, calls a tool, then speaks again)
- **tool_call**: A tool invocation made by the assistant
- **tool_response**: The result returned by the tool

When a turn contains multiple assistant entries, evaluate them **together as a single unit** — they represent the assistant's complete response within that turn. Tool calls and responses between assistant entries explain why the assistant spoke in multiple parts (it was waiting for data). It could also be due to interruptions from the user.

## Understanding Interruption Tags

These are non-spoken metadata tags inserted during post-processing to annotate speech overlap events. They are NOT part of the spoken text.

Tag definitions:
- `[assistant interrupts]` — The assistant started speaking while the user was still talking. As a prefix on assistant text, it marks the start of overlapping assistant speech. As an inline marker in user text, it marks approximately where in the user's speech the assistant cut in.
- `[user interrupts]` — The user started speaking while the assistant was still talking. As a prefix on user text, it marks the start of overlapping user speech. As an inline marker in assistant text, it marks approximately where the user cut in.
- `[likely cut off by user]` — Appears in assistant text. The assistant's speech was probably cut off by the user starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken. Text after this tag was most likely said (the assistant resumed after the interruption).
- `[likely cut off by assistant]` — Appears in user text. The user's speech was probably cut off by the assistant starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[speaker likely cut itself off]` — The speaker likely stopped on its own, possibly after detecting overlap or for other reasons. If the tag appears mid-turn, text after it is what the speaker said after resuming. If the tag appears at the end of the turn, the speaker did not resume in this turn. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[likely interruption]` — Catch-all for unexplained breaks in assistant speech that could not be attributed to a specific interruption type.

**Scope of "text before this tag":** For all four cut-off tags (`[likely cut off by user]`, `[likely cut off by assistant]`, `[speaker likely cut itself off]`, `[likely interruption]`), "text before this tag" means **all text from the start of the turn (or from the previous resumption point) up to the tag** — not just the few adjacent words. This region can span multiple sentences and contain multiple entities (confirmation codes, dollar amounts, names, etc.). Any or all of it may have been silently dropped from the audio. The tag is just a signal that an interruption occurred; it might not be at the right place and do not assume the cut-off was small.


**Key principle:** When interruption tags are present, the assistant may not have been able to finish what it was saying. Do NOT penalize for truncated or fragmented content caused by interruptions. Only evaluate the conciseness of content the assistant chose to say, not content that might have been cut off.

## Instructions
The conversation includes user, assistant, tool_call, and tool_response entries. Rate only the assistant's spoken content. User turns, tool calls, and tool responses are provided for context only.

For each turn that contains assistant content, evaluate whether the assistant's response is appropriately concise and easy to digest when spoken aloud to a human.

The assistant is expected to follow conversational voice guidelines:

- Summarize long lists rather than reading them exhaustively
- Avoid overwhelming the listener with too much information at once
- Spread multiple requests across turns when possible
- Present options conversationally and avoid cramming excessive detail into one turn

When evaluating each turn, consider:
- Does the response get to the point without filler, rambling, or unnecessary content?
- Is all the information relevant and necessary given the conversation context?
- Is the amount of detail reasonable for someone listening to — not reading — the response?
- If the response enumerates options or items (e.g., "Option one is… Option two is…"), does the structure help the user? The volume should not be overwhelming.
- Is the provided information justified by context (e.g., confirming a detail the user may have misheard)? Or is it inappropriate (e.g., excessive itemization or explanation when the user may only care about the end result)?
- Within turns, is repetition avoided? Across turns there may be valid reasons for repetition, but it should usually not occur within a single turn.

1. **Phonetic Confirmation of Codes**

## Understanding the Conversation Format

The conversation is grouped by turn_id. Each turn may contain:
- **user**: What the user said
- **assistant**: What the assistant said (there may be multiple assistant entries within a single turn — e.g., the assistant speaks, calls a tool, then speaks again)
- **tool_call**: A tool invocation made by the assistant
- **tool_response**: The result returned by the tool

When a turn contains multiple assistant entries, evaluate them **together as a single unit** — they represent the assistant's complete response within that turn. Tool calls and responses between assistant entries explain why the assistant spoke in multiple parts (it was waiting for data). It could also be due to interruptions from the user.

## Understanding Interruption Tags

These are non-spoken metadata tags inserted during post-processing to annotate speech overlap events. They are NOT part of the spoken text.

Tag definitions:
- `[assistant interrupts]` — The assistant started speaking while the user was still talking. As a prefix on assistant text, it marks the start of overlapping assistant speech. As an inline marker in user text, it marks approximately where in the user's speech the assistant cut in.
- `[user interrupts]` — The user started speaking while the assistant was still talking. As a prefix on user text, it marks the start of overlapping user speech. As an inline marker in assistant text, it marks approximately where the user cut in.
- `[likely cut off by user]` — Appears in assistant text. The assistant's speech was probably cut off by the user starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken. Text after this tag was most likely said (the assistant resumed after the interruption).
- `[likely cut off by assistant]` — Appears in user text. The user's speech was probably cut off by the assistant starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[speaker likely cut itself off]` — The speaker likely stopped on its own, possibly after detecting overlap or for other reasons. If the tag appears mid-turn, text after it is what the speaker said after resuming. If the tag appears at the end of the turn, the speaker did not resume in this turn. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[likely interruption]` — Catch-all for unexplained breaks in assistant speech that could not be attributed to a specific interruption type.

**Scope of "text before this tag":** For all four cut-off tags (`[likely cut off by user]`, `[likely cut off by assistant]`, `[speaker likely cut itself off]`, `[likely interruption]`), "text before this tag" means **all text from the start of the turn (or from the previous resumption point) up to the tag** — not just the few adjacent words. This region can span multiple sentences and contain multiple entities (confirmation codes, dollar amounts, names, etc.). Any or all of it may have been silently dropped from the audio. The tag is just a signal that an interruption occurred; it might not be at the right place and do not assume the cut-off was small.


**Key principle:** When interruption tags are present, the assistant may not have been able to finish what it was saying. Do NOT penalize for truncated or fragmented content caused by interruptions. Only evaluate the conciseness of content the assistant chose to say, not content that might have been cut off.

## Instructions
The conversation includes user, assistant, tool_call, and tool_response entries. Rate only the assistant's spoken content. User turns, tool calls, and tool responses are provided for context only.

For each turn that contains assistant content, evaluate whether the assistant's response is appropriately concise and easy to digest when spoken aloud to a human.

The assistant is expected to follow conversational voice guidelines:
- Keep responses brief and conversational (typically 2–4 sentences of meaningful conversation content; this may vary by language — some languages have obligatory politeness phrases or structural conventions that naturally add length without adding cognitive load)
- Summarize long lists rather than reading them exhaustively
- Avoid overwhelming the listener with too much information at once
- Spread multiple requests across turns when possible
- Present options conversationally and avoid cramming excessive detail into one turn

## Evaluation Criteria
When evaluating each turn, consider:
- Does the response get to the point without filler, rambling, or unnecessary content?
- Is all the information relevant and necessary given the conversation context?
- Is the amount of detail reasonable for someone listening to — not reading — the response?
- If the response enumerates options or items (e.g., "Option one is… Option two is…"), does the structure help the user? The volume should not be overwhelming.
- Is the provided information justified by context (e.g., confirming a detail the user may have misheard)? Or is it inappropriate (e.g., excessive itemization or explanation when the user may only care about the end result)?
- Within turns, is repetition avoided? Across turns there may be valid reasons for repetition, but it should usually not occur within a single turn.
- Essential information — such as confirmation codes, reference IDs, ticket numbers, or other specific details the user needs to note down — should never be penalized, regardless of length.

## Allowed Exceptions (Voice Interaction Realities)
The assistant may occasionally produce longer turns when the context requires precise information transfer. The following cases should NOT be penalized for verbosity or information density. The turn itself may still be penalized for other reasons.
1. **Phonetic Confirmation of Codes**
- When confirming a confirmation code, reference number, ticket number, or similar identifier, the assistant may spell characters using the NATO phonetic alphabet (e.g., "B as in Bravo, F as in Foxtrot").
- This is especially appropriate when the user previously misheard or asked for clarification.
2. **Reference or Identifier Delivery**
- When providing an identifier the user needs to note down (e.g., a ticket number, reference code, or voucher code), the assistant may read the whole code out loud.
- This information is essential and should not be penalized regardless of length.
3. **End-of-Call Wrap-Up**
- The final assistant turn in a conversation may include a slightly longer recap or confirmation of next steps (e.g., summarizing the action taken, confirming what will be sent or followed up on, thanking the user).
- Minor additional detail in this final wrap-up should not be penalized unless it becomes excessively long or introduces unrelated information.

Important principle: Information given in assistant turns must be short enough for an average person to easily follow in real-time conversation and retain in working memory.

## Failure Modes
When a response is not optimally concise, identify which of the following failure modes are present. A turn may have multiple failure modes.

**verbosity_or_filler**
Contains unnecessary wording, repetition within the same turn, hedging, or explanation beyond what the context requires.
Exception: do NOT flag following of cultural norms, such as obligatory politeness structures (e.g. in Japanese and Korean: keigo, honorifics, set opening/closing phrases).

**excess_information_density**
Presents too many distinct facts, options, numbers, steps, or requests at once, making it difficult for a listener to process in real time. Note: bundling closely related transactional details that the user needs to act on or remember together (e.g., confirming a reference number, date, and one or two key details in a single turn) is expected behavior — only flag this when the volume of information genuinely exceeds what a listener can comfortably retain.

**over_enumeration_or_list_exhaustion**
Reads out long lists instead of summarizing, or presents multiple options with excessive detail rather than inviting follow-up.

**contextually_disproportionate_detail**
Provides more background, clarification, or explanation than the situation warrants.

## Contextual Leniency and Failure Mode Priority
Conciseness should be evaluated with respect to the conversational context. If additional wording or detail is clearly necessary for the user to understand or act on the information, a modest increase in verbosity should be considered acceptable and should NOT be penalized.

If none of the above are present, return an empty list for failure_modes.

## Rating Scale For Each Turn With Assistant Content
- 3 (Highly Concise / No Cognitive Overload) – The response is clear, appropriately scoped for voice, and comfortably digestible in real time. No failure modes are present. A turn that delivers a few closely related facts as part of a single transactional step (e.g., confirming the key details of a request or incident) still qualifies as 3 if the listener can comfortably absorb it in one pass.
- 2 (Adequate but Not Optimally Concise) – One minor failure mode is present, but the response remains reasonably processable in a voice setting and does not meaningfully overwhelm the listener. Reserve this rating for turns where you can identify specific content that should have been omitted or deferred to a later turn — not merely for turns that happen to contain several necessary details.
- 1 (Not Concise / Causes Cognitive Overload) – One or more significant failure modes are present that materially increase cognitive load and would hinder comprehension in a voice conversation.

Provide one entry per turn_id in the conversation.

## Response Format
Provide your response as a valid JSON array, one entry per turn. Each entry must include the turn_id matching the turn number shown in the conversation above.
- If the turn contains assistant content, rate it with 1, 2, or 3.
- If the turn does not contain assistant content (e.g., user-only turn), set rating to null.
[
  {
    "turn_id": <int: the turn number from the conversation>,
    "explanation": "<Detailed analysis in English referencing the evaluation criteria and explicitly linking identified weaknesses to the listed failure modes to justify the selected rating (1–3). Empty string if rating is null.>",
    "failure_modes": ["<failure_mode_1>", "<failure_mode_2>", ...],
    "rating": <int: 1, 2, or 3, or null if no assistant content>
  }
]

If the turn is rated 3 or null, failure_modes must be an empty list: [].

per_turn_explanations.1: The assistant delivers a long, procedural monologue before getting the needed inputs. It front-loads identity-verification rationale, eligibility rules, multiple extension types, and duration options, then asks for four different identifiers at once. In a voice setting this is hard to hold in working memory and ignores the user's need to proceed step-by-step, creating cognitive overload.
per_turn_explanations.2: The assistant appropriately accepts the user's preference to go step-by-step and confirms the NPI, then asks for the remaining items. However, it adds extra process narration (multiple future steps) that isn't necessary at this moment and slightly over-repeats how it will proceed, making it a bit longer than needed for voice.
per_turn_explanations.3: It clearly confirms authentication and requests the single missing item (state license number), which is good turn-scoping. But it adds unnecessary details for the listener (spelling out/reading the employee ID and explaining internal handling) and extra procedural framing. The core request could be delivered more succinctly.
per_turn_explanations.4: Reading back the license number is appropriate for voice accuracy. The response becomes less concise when it adds multiple next-step promises (status, expiration, type, existing extensions, eligibility check) and then re-introduces extension type and duration options before the record is even retrieved. This increases density more than the context requires, but remains broadly followable.
per_turn_explanations.5: This turn is very long and reads an exhaustive list of fields, including many 'empty/none' items, which is unnecessary for the user’s decision-making. It repeats identifiers and enumerates numerous record attributes instead of summarizing the key points (active, eligible, no holds, no existing extension). per_turn_explanations.6: It confirms submission success and provides the essential case ID (important and not penalized). However, the recap is longer than necessary for voice: it repeats multiple identifiers, re-reads the supervisor NPI twice (including an English slip and correction), and lists many details that the user likely doesn’t need after submission. ## Understanding the Conversation Format

The conversation is grouped by turn_id. Each turn may contain:
- **user**: What the user said
- **assistant**: What the assistant said (there may be multiple assistant entries within a single turn — e.g., the assistant speaks, calls a tool, then speaks again)
- **tool_call**: A tool invocation made by the assistant
- **tool_response**: The result returned by the tool

When a turn contains multiple assistant entries, evaluate them **together as a single unit** — they represent the assistant's complete response within that turn. Tool calls and responses between assistant entries explain why the assistant spoke in multiple parts (it was waiting for data). It could also be due to interruptions from the user.

## Understanding Interruption Tags

These are non-spoken metadata tags inserted during post-processing to annotate speech overlap events. They are NOT part of the spoken text.

Tag definitions:
- `[assistant interrupts]` — The assistant started speaking while the user was still talking. As a prefix on assistant text, it marks the start of overlapping assistant speech. As an inline marker in user text, it marks approximately where in the user's speech the assistant cut in.
- `[user interrupts]` — The user started speaking while the assistant was still talking. As a prefix on user text, it marks the start of overlapping user speech. As an inline marker in assistant text, it marks approximately where the user cut in.
- `[likely cut off by user]` — Appears in assistant text. The assistant's speech was probably cut off by the user starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken. Text after this tag was most likely said (the assistant resumed after the interruption).
- `[likely cut off by assistant]` — Appears in user text. The user's speech was probably cut off by the assistant starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[speaker likely cut itself off]` — The speaker likely stopped on its own, possibly after detecting overlap or for other reasons. If the tag appears mid-turn, text after it is what the speaker said after resuming. If the tag appears at the end of the turn, the speaker did not resume in this turn. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[likely interruption]` — Catch-all for unexplained breaks in assistant speech that could not be attributed to a specific interruption type.

**Scope of "text before this tag":** For all four cut-off tags (`[likely cut off by user]`, `[likely cut off by assistant]`, `[speaker likely cut itself off]`, `[likely interruption]`), "text before this tag" means **all text from the start of the turn (or from the previous resumption point) up to the tag** — not just the few adjacent words. This region can span multiple sentences and contain multiple entities (confirmation codes, dollar amounts, names, etc.). Any or all of it may have been silently dropped from the audio. The tag is just a signal that an interruption occurred; it might not be at the right place and do not assume the cut-off was small.


**Key principle:** When interruption tags are present, the assistant may not have been able to finish what it was saying. Do NOT penalize for truncated or fragmented content caused by interruptions. Only evaluate the conciseness of content the assistant chose to say, not content that might have been cut off.

## Instructions
The conversation includes user, assistant, tool_call, and tool_response entries. Rate only the assistant's spoken content. User turns, tool calls, and tool responses are provided for context only.

For each turn that contains assistant content, evaluate whether the assistant's response is appropriately concise and easy to digest when spoken aloud to a human.

The assistant is expected to follow conversational voice guidelines:
- Keep responses brief and conversational (typically 2–4 sentences of meaningful conversation content; this may vary by language — some languages have obligatory politeness phrases or structural conventions that naturally add length without adding cognitive load)
- Summarize long lists rather than reading them exhaustively
- Avoid overwhelming the listener with too much information at once
- Spread multiple requests across turns when possible
- Present options conversationally and avoid cramming excessive detail into one turn

## Evaluation Criteria
When evaluating each turn, consider:
- Does the response get to the point without filler, rambling, or unnecessary content?
- Is all the information relevant and necessary given the conversation context?
- Is the amount of detail reasonable for someone listening to — not reading — the response?
- If the response enumerates options or items (e.g., "Option one is… Option two is…"), does the structure help the user? The volume should not be overwhelming.
- Is the provided information justified by context (e.g., confirming a detail the user may have misheard)? Or is it inappropriate (e.g., excessive itemization or explanation when the user may only care about the end result)?
- Within turns, is repetition avoided? Across turns there may be valid reasons for repetition, but it should usually not occur within a single turn.
- Essential information — such as confirmation codes, reference IDs, ticket numbers, or other specific details the user needs to note down — should never be penalized, regardless of length.

## Allowed Exceptions (Voice Interaction Realities)
The assistant may occasionally produce longer turns when the context requires precise information transfer. The following cases should NOT be penalized for verbosity or information density. The turn itself may still be penalized for other reasons.
1. **Phonetic Confirmation of Codes**
- When confirming a confirmation code, reference number, ticket number, or similar identifier, the assistant may spell characters using the NATO phonetic alphabet (e.g., "B as in Bravo, F as in Foxtrot").
- This is especially appropriate when the user previously misheard or asked for clarification.
2. **Reference or Identifier Delivery**
- When providing an identifier the user needs to note down (e.g., a ticket number, reference code, or voucher code), the assistant may read the whole code out loud.
- This information is essential and should not be penalized regardless of length.
3. **End-of-Call Wrap-Up**
- The final assistant turn in a conversation may include a slightly longer recap or confirmation of next steps (e.g., summarizing the action taken, confirming what will be sent or followed up on, thanking the user).
- Minor additional detail in this final wrap-up should not be penalized unless it becomes excessively long or introduces unrelated information.

Important principle: Information given in assistant turns must be short enough for an average person to easily follow in real-time conversation and retain in working memory.

## Failure Modes
When a response is not optimally concise, identify which of the following failure modes are present. A turn may have multiple failure modes.

**verbosity_or_filler**
Contains unnecessary wording, repetition within the same turn, hedging, or explanation beyond what the context requires.
Exception: do NOT flag following of cultural norms, such as obligatory politeness structures (e.g. in Japanese and Korean: keigo, honorifics, set opening/closing phrases).

**excess_information_density**
Presents too many distinct facts, options, numbers, steps, or requests at once, making it difficult for a listener to process in real time. Note: bundling closely related transactional details that the user needs to act on or remember together (e.g., confirming a reference number, date, and one or two key details in a single turn) is expected behavior — only flag this when the volume of information genuinely exceeds what a listener can comfortably retain.

**over_enumeration_or_list_exhaustion**
Reads out long lists instead of summarizing, or presents multiple options with excessive detail rather than inviting follow-up.

**contextually_disproportionate_detail**
Provides more background, clarification, or explanation than the situation warrants.

## Contextual Leniency and Failure Mode Priority
Conciseness should be evaluated with respect to the conversational context. If additional wording or detail is clearly necessary for the user to understand or act on the information, a modest increase in verbosity should be considered acceptable and should NOT be penalized.

If none of the above are present, return an empty list for failure_modes.

## Rating Scale For Each Turn With Assistant Content
- 3 (Highly Concise / No Cognitive Overload) – The response is clear, appropriately scoped for voice, and comfortably digestible in real time. No failure modes are present. A turn that delivers a few closely related facts as part of a single transactional step (e.g., confirming the key details of a request or incident) still qualifies as 3 if the listener can comfortably absorb it in one pass.
- 2 (Adequate but Not Optimally Concise) – One minor failure mode is present, but the response remains reasonably processable in a voice setting and does not meaningfully overwhelm the listener. Reserve this rating for turns where you can identify specific content that should have been omitted or deferred to a later turn — not merely for turns that happen to contain several necessary details.
- 1 (Not Concise / Causes Cognitive Overload) – One or more significant failure modes are present that materially increase cognitive load and would hinder comprehension in a voice conversation.

Provide one entry per turn_id in the conversation.

## Response Format
Provide your response as a valid JSON array, one entry per turn. Each entry must include the turn_id matching the turn number shown in the conversation above.
- If the turn contains assistant content, rate it with 1, 2, or 3.
- If the turn does not contain assistant content (e.g., user-only turn), set rating to null.
[
  {
    "turn_id": <int: the turn number from the conversation>,
    "explanation": "<Detailed analysis in English referencing the evaluation criteria and explicitly linking identified weaknesses to the listed failure modes to justify the selected rating (1–3). Empty string if rating is null.>",
    "failure_modes": ["<failure_mode_1>", "<failure_mode_2>", ...],
    "rating": <int: 1, 2, or 3, or null if no assistant content>
  }
]

If the turn is rated 3 or null, failure_modes must be an empty list: [].

## Understanding the Conversation Format

The conversation is grouped by turn_id. Each turn may contain:
- **user**: What the user said
- **assistant**: What the assistant said (there may be multiple assistant entries within a single turn — e.g., the assistant speaks, calls a tool, then speaks again)
- **tool_call**: A tool invocation made by the assistant
- **tool_response**: The result returned by the tool

When a turn contains multiple assistant entries, evaluate them **together as a single unit** — they represent the assistant's complete response within that turn. Tool calls and responses between assistant entries explain why the assistant spoke in multiple parts (it was waiting for data). It could also be due to interruptions from the user.

## Understanding Interruption Tags

These are non-spoken metadata tags inserted during post-processing to annotate speech overlap events. They are NOT part of the spoken text.

Tag definitions:
- `[assistant interrupts]` — The assistant started speaking while the user was still talking. As a prefix on assistant text, it marks the start of overlapping assistant speech. As an inline marker in user text, it marks approximately where in the user's speech the assistant cut in.
- `[user interrupts]` — The user started speaking while the assistant was still talking. As a prefix on user text, it marks the start of overlapping user speech. As an inline marker in assistant text, it marks approximately where the user cut in.
- `[likely cut off by user]` — Appears in assistant text. The assistant's speech was probably cut off by the user starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken. Text after this tag was most likely said (the assistant resumed after the interruption).
- `[likely cut off by assistant]` — Appears in user text. The user's speech was probably cut off by the assistant starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[speaker likely cut itself off]` — The speaker likely stopped on its own, possibly after detecting overlap or for other reasons. If the tag appears mid-turn, text after it is what the speaker said after resuming. If the tag appears at the end of the turn, the speaker did not resume in this turn. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken.
- `[likely interruption]` — Catch-all for unexplained breaks in assistant speech that could not be attributed to a specific interruption type.

**Scope of "text before this tag":** For all four cut-off tags (`[likely cut off by user]`, `[likely cut off by assistant]`, `[speaker likely cut itself off]`, `[likely interruption]`), "text before this tag" means **all text from the start of the turn (or from the previous resumption point) up to the tag** — not just the few adjacent words. This region can span multiple sentences and contain multiple entities (confirmation codes, dollar amounts, names, etc.). Any or all of it may have been silently dropped from the audio. The tag is just a signal that an interruption occurred; it might not be at the right place and do not assume the cut-off was small.


**Key principle:** When interruption tags are present, the assistant may not have been able to finish what it was saying. Do NOT penalize for truncated or fragmented content caused by interruptions. Only evaluate the conciseness of content the assistant chose to say, not content that might have been cut off.

## Instructions
The conversation includes user, assistant, tool_call, and tool_response entries. Rate only the assistant's spoken content. User turns, tool calls, and tool responses are provided for context only.

For each turn that contains assistant content, evaluate whether the assistant's response is appropriately concise and easy to digest when spoken aloud to a human.

The assistant is expected to follow conversational voice guidelines:
- Keep responses brief and conversational (typically 2–4 sentences of meaningful conversation content; this may vary by language — some languages have obligatory politeness phrases or structural conventions that naturally add length without adding cognitive load)
- Summarize long lists rather than reading them exhaustively
- Avoid overwhelming the listener with too much information at once
- Spread multiple requests across turns when possible
- Present options conversationally and avoid cramming excessive detail into one turn

## Evaluation Criteria
When evaluating each turn, consider:
- Does the response get to the point without filler, rambling, or unnecessary content?
- Is all the information relevant and necessary given the conversation context?
- Is the amount of detail reasonable for someone listening to — not reading — the response?
- If the response enumerates options or items (e.g., "Option one is… Option two is…"), does the structure help the user? The volume should not be overwhelming.
- Is the provided information justified by context (e.g., confirming a detail the user may have misheard)? Or is it inappropriate (e.g., excessive itemization or explanation when the user may only care about the end result)?
- Within turns, is repetition avoided? Across turns there may be valid reasons for repetition, but it should usually not occur within a single turn.
- Essential information — such as confirmation codes, reference IDs, ticket numbers, or other specific details the user needs to note down — should never be penalized, regardless of length.

## Allowed Exceptions (Voice Interaction Realities)
The assistant may occasionally produce longer turns when the context requires precise information transfer. The following cases should NOT be penalized for verbosity or information density. The turn itself may still be penalized for other reasons.
1. **Phonetic Confirmation of Codes**
- When confirming a confirmation code, reference number, ticket number, or similar identifier, the assistant may spell characters using the NATO phonetic alphabet (e.g., "B as in Bravo, F as in Foxtrot").
- This is especially appropriate when the user previously misheard or asked for clarification.
2. **Reference or Identifier Delivery**
- When providing an identifier the user needs to note down (e.g., a ticket number, reference code, or voucher code), the assistant may read the whole code out loud.
- This information is essential and should not be penalized regardless of length.
3. **End-of-Call Wrap-Up**
- The final assistant turn in a conversation may include a slightly longer recap or confirmation of next steps (e.g., summarizing the action taken, confirming what will be sent or followed up on, thanking the user).
- Minor additional detail in this final wrap-up should not be penalized unless it becomes excessively long or introduces unrelated information.

Important principle: Information given in assistant turns must be short enough for an average person to easily follow in real-time conversation and retain in working memory.

## Failure Modes
When a response is not optimally concise, identify which of the following failure modes are present. A turn may have multiple failure modes.

**verbosity_or_filler**
Contains unnecessary wording, repetition within the same turn, hedging, or explanation beyond what the context requires.
Exception: do NOT flag following of cultural norms, such as obligatory politeness structures (e.g. in Japanese and Korean: keigo, honorifics, set opening/closing phrases).

**excess_information_density**
Presents too many distinct facts, options, numbers, steps, or requests at once, making it difficult for a listener to process in real time. Note: bundling closely related transactional details that the user needs to act on or remember together (e.g., confirming a reference number, date, and one or two key details in a single turn) is expected behavior — only flag this when the volume of information genuinely exceeds what a listener can comfortably retain.

**over_enumeration_or_list_exhaustion**
Reads out long lists instead of summarizing, or presents multiple options with excessive detail rather than inviting follow-up.

**contextually_disproportionate_detail**
Provides more background, clarification, or explanation than the situation warrants.

## Contextual Leniency and Failure Mode Priority
Conciseness should be evaluated with respect to the conversational context. If additional wording or detail is clearly necessary for the user to understand or act on the information, a modest increase in verbosity should be considered acceptable and should NOT be penalized.

If none of the above are present, return an empty list for failure_modes.

## Rating Scale For Each Turn With Assistant Content
- 3 (Highly Concise / No Cognitive Overload) – The response is clear, appropriately scoped for voice, and comfortably digestible in real time. No failure modes are present. A turn that delivers a few closely related facts as part of a single transactional step (e.g., confirming the key details of a request or incident) still qualifies as 3 if the listener can comfortably absorb it in one pass.
- 2 (Adequate but Not Optimally Concise) – One minor failure mode is present, but the response remains reasonably processable in a voice setting and does not meaningfully overwhelm the listener. Reserve this rating for turns where you can identify specific content that should have been omitted or deferred to a later turn — not merely for turns that happen to contain several necessary details.
- 1 (Not Concise / Causes Cognitive Overload) – One or more significant failure modes are present that materially increase cognitive load and would hinder comprehension in a voice conversation.

Provide one entry per turn_id in the conversation.

## Response Format
Provide your response as a valid JSON array, one entry per turn. Each entry must include the turn_id matching the turn number shown in the conversation above.
- If the turn contains assistant content, rate it with 1, 2, or 3.
- If the turn does not contain assistant content (e.g., user-only turn), set rating to null.
[
  {
    "turn_id": <int: the turn number from the conversation>,
    "explanation": "<Detailed analysis in English referencing the evaluation criteria and explicitly linking identified weaknesses to the listed failure modes to justify the selected rating (1–3). Empty string if rating is null.>",
    "failure_modes": ["<failure_mode_1>", "<failure_mode_2>", ...],
    "rating": <int: 1, 2, or 3, or null if no assistant content>
  }
]

If the turn is rated 3 or null, failure_modes must be an empty list: [].

conversation_trace.content: Bonjour, j’ai besoin d’aide pour demander une prolongation temporaire de ma licence.

Bonjour, je peux vous aider avec cela, et comme il s’agit d’une demande liée à une licence professionnelle, je dois d’abord faire une vérification d’identité de prestataire avant de pouvoir consulter ou modifier le dossier. Pour ce type de demande, j’ai besoin de trois éléments précis, et je vais les utiliser uniquement pour l’authentification afin de protéger votre dossier. Merci de me donner votre numéro N P I, votre code d’établissement principal, et votre code P I N à quatre chiffres. Veuillez les dire lentement, et pour éviter toute erreur de transcription, vous pouvez aussi les énoncer par petits groupes. Une fois que j’aurai ces trois éléments, je pourrai vérifier votre identité, consulter l’état actuel de votre licence, confirmer si une prolongation est autorisée selon la date d’expiration, puis vous expliquer toutes les options possibles de prolongation temporaire.

D’accord.  
Mon numéro N P I est 3 6 1 5 5 0 7 1 4 3.  
Mon code d’établissement est T O U – 7 7 A.  
Mon code P I N est 6 3 1 0.

Merci, Dr Lefèvre. Votre vérification de prestataire est bien réussie, donc je peux maintenant avancer avec la demande de prolongation de licence en toute conformité. Comme une prolongation de licence ne nécessite pas de code à usage unique supplémentaire, la vérification que nous venons de faire suffit pour cette demande. Avant de pouvoir soumettre quoi que ce soit, la procédure m’oblige à consulter d’abord le dossier actuel de la licence, puis à vérifier l’admissibilité de la prolongation, parce qu’une prolongation n’est possible que si la licence n’est pas déjà expirée, n’a pas de demande en attente, et se trouve dans la fenêtre autorisée de soixante jours avant expiration. J’ai donc besoin maintenant d’un seul identifiant supplémentaire, à savoir le numéro exact de la licence d’État concernée; merci de me le lire lentement, et je vous le relirai ensuite pour confirmation avant de l’utiliser. Ensuite, pour gagner du temps et éviter de vous faire répéter les choses plus tard, vous pouvez aussi me dire en même temps si vous souhaitez, en principe, une prolongation provisoire ou une prolongation supervisée, ainsi que la durée souhaitée parmi trente, soixante, ou quatre-vingt-dix jours; si vous choisissez la formule supervisée, j’aurai également besoin du numéro N P I du médecin superviseur, qui doit être différent du vôtre.

Le numéro de ma licence d’État est O H – R N – 1 5 1 1 4 6 3 1.  
Je souhaite une prolongation provisoire de trente jours.

tool_response.message: An extension request is already pending for this license

conversation_trace.content:
Merci. Je vous relis d’abord l’identifiant que vous avez donné, parce que c’est le type d’élément où une seule erreur de caractère peut viser le mauvais dossier : j’ai bien entendu O H, tiret, R N, tiret, un cinq un un quatre six trois un, donc la licence O H tiret R N tiret un cinq un un quatre six trois un. J’ai consulté le dossier actuel de cette licence et j’ai aussi vérifié l’admissibilité à une nouvelle prolongation. Voici ce que le système me retourne, de façon complète : il s’agit d’une licence de type infirmier ou infirmière autorisé, dans l’État de l’Ohio, avec le numéro O H tiret R N tiret un cinq un un quatre six trois un; la date d’expiration enregistrée est le vingt juin deux mille vingt-six; le statut actuel de la licence est actif; il n’y a pas de blocage pour enquête; mais il existe déjà une demande de prolongation en attente. Le dossier indique même les détails de cette demande en cours : il s’agit d’une prolongation provisoire, pour trente jours, sans médecin superviseur, et le numéro de dossier associé est C A S E, tiret, L I C, tiret, deux six zéro deux six trois.

Comme résultat, je ne peux pas soumettre une nouvelle prolongation aujourd’hui, parce que la vérification d’admissibilité bloque explicitement toute nouvelle demande lorsqu’une prolongation est déjà en attente. Autrement dit, votre demande correspond déjà exactement au type que vous m’avez indiqué maintenant, à savoir une prolongation provisoire de trente jours, mais elle semble avoir déjà été déposée dans le système. Je ne peux donc ni créer un doublon, ni la modifier par cette voie tant que cette demande reste pendante. La bonne nouvelle, c’est que votre licence elle-même apparaît encore active, avec une expiration au vingt juin deux mille vingt-six, et qu’aucun indicateur d’enquête n’est présent dans le dossier.

Si vous le souhaitez, je peux maintenant vous aider de deux façons : soit je vous résume simplement les informations de la demande déjà en attente pour que vous les notiez, soit je peux vous proposer un transfert vers un agent humain afin qu’il examine le statut de la demande en cours, surtout si vous pensez ne pas avoir soumis cette prolongation vous-même ou si vous avez besoin d’une exception ou d’un suivi accéléré. Si vous préférez le transfert, je m’en charge et je transmettrai le contexte complet, y compris le numéro de dossier C A S E tiret L I C tiret deux six zéro deux six trois.

D’accord, donc je ne peux pas déposer de nouvelle demande.  
Juste pour confirmer : ça veut bien dire qu’aucune action supplémentaire n’est nécessaire de ma part pour obtenir cette prolongation provisoire de trente jours déjà déposée ?

Oui, d’après ce que le système m’a montré, une demande de prolongation provisoire de trente jours est déjà enregistrée comme étant en attente, donc vous n’avez pas besoin de déposer une deuxième demande. Je veux toutefois être très précis pour ne pas vous induire en erreur : je peux confirmer qu’aucune nouvelle soumission n’est nécessaire de votre part par téléphone pour créer cette prolongation, parce elle existe déjà dans le dossier. En revanche, je ne peux pas confirmer à partir de cet écran seul qu’aucun suivi complémentaire ne vous sera jamais demandé ensuite par l’équipe de credentialing, car mon accès ici montre l’existence et les détails de la demande en attente, mais pas la liste d’éventuels documents additionnels qu’un examinateur pourrait réclamer plus tard pendant la revue. Ce que je peux vous dire avec certitude, c’est que le dossier actuel affiche une licence active, expirant le vingt juin deux mille vingt-six, sans blocage d’enquête, avec une prolongation provisoire de trente jours déjà pendante sous le numéro C A S E, tiret, L I C, tiret, deux six zéro deux six trois.

Donc, en pratique, la prochaine étape normale est l’examen de cette demande déjà soumise, et non une nouvelle action de dépôt de votre part. Si vous voulez une confirmation plus forte sur l’absence totale d’action restante, le moyen le plus sûr serait un suivi avec un agent humain ou directement avec l’équipe de credentialing, afin qu’ils vérifient s’il y a des pièces manquantes ou des conditions en suspens sur ce dossier précis. Je peux vous transférer maintenant si vous souhaitez cette vérification de statut plus poussée. Sinon, vous pouvez simplement conserver le numéro de dossier et attendre la suite du traitement. Pour bien clôturer ce que nous avons fait aujourd’hui, le numéro de dossier concerné est C A S E tiret L I C tiret deux six zéro deux six trois, et nous avons confirmé qu’une prolongation provisoire de trente jours est déjà en attente pour votre licence O H tiret R N tiret un cinq un un quatre six trois un.

per_turn_explanations.1: The assistant front-loads a lot of procedural explanation (why identity verification is required, how the data will be used, what will happen after verification) before simply requesting the three needed items. It also asks for three identifiers in one long, multi-clause paragraph, increasing real-time cognitive load in a voice setting. This is more detail than necessary at this moment and could have been broken into shorter turns (ask for NPI first, then facility code, then PIN).
per_turn_explanations.2: After successful verification, the assistant adds extra compliance commentary and then delivers a lengthy policy-like eligibility explanation plus multiple requests and choices at once (license number, extension type, duration options, and possibly a supervisor NPI). This bundles too many decision points into a single spoken turn and includes details (e.g., the 60-day window rules) that could be summarized or deferred until after pulling the record.
per_turn_explanations.3: The assistant appropriately confirms the license identifier, but then reads back an exhaustive set of record fields (type, state, expiration date, status, investigation hold) and repeats the same conclusion multiple times (cannot submit a new extension because one is pending). It also spells out the case ID and repeats it several times, plus offers multiple next-step options in a long block. While providing the case ID is justified, the rest could be condensed to: 'You already have a pending 30-day provisional extension; no duplicate can be filed. Here’s the case ID; I can transfer you or summarize it.'
per_turn_explanations.4: The assistant answers the user’s confirmation question but does so with repeated phrasing and extended caveats, re-stating multiple record details (license active, expiration date, no investigation hold, extension details) that are not necessary to address whether the user must take action now. The cautious disclaimer about possible future document requests is reasonable, but it is longer than needed and the case ID is repeated again. Overall still understandable, but not optimally concise for voice.

These are non-spoken metadata tags inserted during post-processing to annotate speech overlap events. They are NOT part of the spoken text.

- `[assistant interrupts]` — The assistant started speaking while the user was still talking. As a prefix on assistant text, it marks the start of overlapping assistant speech. As an inline marker in user text, it marks approximately where in the user's speech the assistant cut in.
- `[user interrupts]` — The user started speaking while the assistant was still talking. As a prefix on user text, it marks the start of overlapping user speech. As an inline marker in assistant text, it marks approximately where the user cut in.
- `[likely cut off by user]` — Appears in assistant text. The assistant's speech was probably cut off by the user starting to speak. Text before this tag may not have been fully spoken. Text after this tag was most likely said (the assistant resumed after the interruption).

conversation_trace.content: Bonjour, j’appelle au sujet du changement d’un de mes horaires de travail.

Bonjour, bien sûr, je peux vous aider avec cela, et merci de m’avoir précisé qu’il s’agit d’un changement lié à votre horaire de travail. Comme votre demande concerne la planification du personnel, je dois d’abord vérifier votre identité avant de pouvoir consulter ou modifier quoi que ce soit dans votre dossier. Je préfère le faire tout de suite pour protéger vos informations et pour que nous puissions ensuite avancer sans interruption sur la bonne procédure, qu’il s’agisse d’un échange de quart, d’une correction liée à un horaire déjà travaillé, d’une disponibilité de garde, ou d’un autre ajustement de planning. Une fois la vérification faite, je pourrai vous expliquer exactement les options qui existent et lesquelles s’appliquent à votre situation précise.

Pour commencer, j’ai besoin de deux éléments, et vous pouvez me les donner dans la même réponse pour aller plus vite. D’abord, votre identifiant employé, au format E M P suivi de six chiffres. Ensuite, votre date de naissance, au format année, mois, jour, par exemple dix-neuf cent quatre-vingt-six, zéro trois, zéro quatre. Et pendant que nous y sommes, pour que je puisse orienter la suite correctement dès que vous serez authentifié, dites-moi aussi en quelques mots quel type de changement d’horaire vous souhaitez faire, par exemple un échange de quart avec un collègue, une correction de paie liée à un quart, une demande de disponibilité d’astreinte, ou autre chose.

Oui. Mon identifiant, c’est E M P huit cinq zéro huit zéro zéro.  
Ma date de naissance, c’est mille neuf cent quatre-vingt-onze, zéro huit, vingt-deux. Et c’est pour un échange de quart avec un collègue.

Merci beaucoup, Monsieur Gilles Fournier. Votre identité est bien vérifiée, donc nous pouvons maintenant avancer sur votre demande d’échange de quart en toute sécurité. Comme il s’agit d’un changement de planning, je vais devoir d’abord identifier précisément le quart concerné, puis vérifier s’il est admissible à un échange, et ensuite confirmer que votre collègue possède bien toutes les certifications requises pour l’unité de ce quart. Je vous explique cela parce que je ne peux pas enregistrer l’échange directement sans ces contrôles préalables, et cela évite tout problème de couverture de service ou de conformité.

Pour continuer efficacement en une seule étape, j’ai besoin de tous les éléments suivants dans votre prochaine réponse. D’abord, la date du quart que vous souhaitez échanger, puis son heure de début, en précisant bien matin ou soir si nécessaire, afin que je puisse construire l’identifiant du quart et vous le relire avant de l’utiliser. Ensuite, j’ai besoin de l’identifiant employé de votre collègue, qui est une valeur distincte du vôtre et qui doit aussi être exact au chiffre près. Si vous le souhaitez, vous pouvez également me dire, en une phrase, si vous savez déjà que ce quart est encore à venir et qu’il n’a pas déjà été modifié, même si je vais le vérifier de mon côté. Donnez-moi donc, dans le même message, la date du quart, l’heure de début, et l’identifiant employé de votre collègue.

La date du quart, c’est le quatorze septembre deux mille vingt-six.  
L’heure de début, c’est trois heures de l’après-midi. Et l’identifiant de mon collègue, c’est E M P sept huit un quatre cinq trois.

Merci, j’ai bien noté les éléments que vous venez de me donner, et je vais d’abord reformuler l’identifiant du quart avant toute consultation, parce que c’est exactement le type d’information où une seule erreur de date ou d’heure peut pointer vers le mauvais dossier. À partir de la date du quatorze septembre deux mille vingt-six et d’une heure de début à trois heures de l’après-midi, l’identifiant du quart que je construis est le suivant : S H F, tiret, deux zéro deux six zéro neuf un quatre, tiret, un cinq zéro zéro. Autrement dit, cela donne SHF-20260914-1500. Et pour votre collègue, j’ai noté l’identifiant employé EMP781453.

Avant que je lance les vérifications du quart et de l’admissibilité à l’échange, je veux simplement que vous me confirmiez en une seule réponse que ces deux identifiants sont exacts tels que je viens de les relire : d’une part SHF-20260914-1500 pour le quart, et d’autre part EMP781453 pour votre collègue.
